text:
We’re thrilled to invest in Phaze.

@Phaze_in is a high-performance remote desktop solution for giving humans and agents a local-like experience on remote workstations. It’s the best solution for interactive, latency-sensitive workloads, and it was designed from the ground up for working with agents, which makes compatibility, management and administration seamless.

It’s not a surprise Phaze is as good as it is given the team behind it. @boxerbk and Chris Dickson, the founders of Phaze, previously built Parsec, which at the time was the leading remote desktop solution for graphics-intensive applications.

We’re very excited to be working with this team again to bring desktops and applications to agents. And of course to humans too.

By @martin_casado
author: a16z
quoted_text:
Today we’re announcing an $8.75M seed round for Phaze.

Companies aren’t ready for how many computers people and AI agents are about to need. And it’s happening just as computer prices are up 3x.

Chris and I spent years building Parsec to make a computer thousands of miles away feel like it’s sitting right in front of you. We sold that company, and we’re starting over because people aren’t the only users of computers anymore.

Now, agents need access to real computers to run applications, test software, and get work done. They need to work alongside people, hand off control when necessary, and operate within the security policies companies already have in place. And companies need to start managing computers like infrastructure.

That’s why we’re building @Phaze_in: secure, high-performance access to computers, wherever those machines happen to be.

An engineer can connect to a CAD workstation from any device and forget about being physically stuck at that workstation. A video editor can ask an AI agent to connect to a render machine to monitor and fix broken renders. An IT support person can fix multiple machines at the same time with an AI agent connecting to employees’ computers. If the agent needs help, it can hand control back to the technician in the same session.

We loved working with the firms who backed Parsec, so we’re running it back. Our Seed round is led by @martin_casado at @a16z, with @bryce at @indievc, @davidbeisel at @NextViewVC, @BenjLerer at @LererHippeau, and @Ryann_Lai at @makersfundvc.

text:
Some personal news: I joined Lucid Computing (@LucidCompute) as Director of Research Partnerships & Standards.

My core focus will be to help foster more open source collaboration across the AI verification ecosystem, between the many teams working on similar / adjacent topics and pieces of technology.

I am so excited to finally be able to share this next chapter of my career. As I posted recently, I have been completely obsessed with AI safety.

It accelerated in March this year, when @ercwl put me in a group chat with @Kristian_Ronn. At the time, I was actively exploring the use of Zero Knowledge Proofs for critical AI use cases (mostly in insurance, defense, healthcare and robotics).

We immediately had great vibes together. We shared the same vision and the same enthusiasm, and we both saw AI safety as the most important thing humanity could work on.

Since then, I have met Greg, Lucid’s co-founder and CTO, and it was the same kind of connection, the same feeling of a shared vision and mission. And everyone I have met at Lucid since I joined is the same kind of person: talented, mission driven, and with a deep willingness to have a real impact with our work.

It’s a real honor to join them all on this epic journey.

I genuinely believe that cryptography and math are our only hope of avoiding a dystopian, totalitarian world with massive concentration of power, gatekeeping of intelligence, and abuse in many forms.

The beauty of cryptography and math, and Zero Knowledge Proofs in particular, is that they are tools that can break the asymmetry of power. This is precisely what we need for AI right now.

We also need solutions designed for the most adversarial conditions possible, including resisting superpowerful nation-state actors. That’s the only way to aim for credible international treaties to “pace AI”.

The threats and risks are immense, and AI safety is probably the greatest challenge humanity has ever faced. Despite that, I am hopeful, and I remain optimistic that we still have the power to change course. This will inevitably require cooperation and collaboration at many levels.

From what I have seen, there is a strong appetite for more open source collaboration in the AI verification ecosystem. That’s a great starting point, and I have high hopes that we can stimulate and nurture a very healthy, collaborative environment, with no zero-sum mentality. 

We need to join forces, more than ever.

The space is way too small today. It will have to grow massively over the coming months, and I am sure it will. That makes it even more important to build solid foundations and a strong culture in the ecosystem, so it can grow and scale the right way.

I will do my very best to help build that collaborative environment. I love building in public, I am an open source maxi, and I am used to working with many entities across distributed ecosystems.

The topics and primitives where I will focus and facilitate open source collaboration:
- ZK for provable inference
- Proof of exhaustion schemes
- Workload classification, via different techniques
- Hardware roots of trust, TEEs, hardware formal verification
- Formal verification

If you are working on any of these in AI verification, I would love to connect and see how we can join forces on our shared mission.

If you are not working on AI verification (or AI safety more broadly): first, you are missing out. Second, we need you. We need a lot more talent working on these problems.

Lastly, I will work on public communication and educational material about AI verification and our work at Lucid. More on this very soon. 

Follow @LucidCompute and @Kristian_Ronn, and stay tuned.

Let's build AI using tech to make it more verifiable and safer!

text: Every word of this is 💯💯💯
author: DonaldJTrumpJr
quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

存储股这波大顶，我不是猜的，是按框架定位的。

6/22-6/25 美光 1,257、闪迪 2,382、海力士 1,978 同步见顶，至今 -33%~-41%。我的见顶框架四个信号，当时亮了三个：

1️⃣ 合约价涨幅斜率崩了。DRAM 季度环比 Q1 +93~98% → Q2 +58~63% → Q3 预估只剩 +13~18%。股价定价的从来不是价格水平，是斜率。斜率拐头，故事就完了。

2️⃣ 供给端全面反击。美光 2,500 亿美元建厂、三星提前扩产、海力士加速下设备单、长鑫上市。一个行业人人抢着扩产的时候，周期顶就不远了。

3️⃣ 利好钝化——最响的信号。业绩预告 +1099%、+3200% 的公司直接跌停；海力士 ADR 七倍超购、首日 +12.8%，第二天韩股 -10%。庆典即顶点：利好砸不出新高，就是在派发。

4️⃣ HBM 砍单（没触发）。这恰恰说明产业还没顶，但股价先顶了。2018 年美光股价 5 月见顶，DRAM 合约价 Q3 才见顶——股价领先产业 2-4 个季度。等产业数据变坏再跑，晚了。

盘面也在自己说话：反弹高点三连降（1,257→1,050→1,007），每次反弹卖压来得更早，教科书级派发结构。

周期股赚的是斜率的钱，不是景气的钱。景气最好的那天，往往就是股价最贵的那天。

text:
63 亿美元的损失，放在整个行业都是一次沉重的警钟。币安愿意承担责任、公开复盘，值得肯定，作为一次教训，未来应该也会有更多持续、透明、可验证的整改。

同时更大视角来看这件事，我觉得面对越来越复杂的攻击，行业需要的是合作，而不是内耗。

希望这次事件最终推动整个行业的安全标准向前一步。

也能让大家更加安心的把资产放在 CEX
author: Bitwux
quoted_text:
有些话，不吐不快！

63 亿美元，绝不只是一个小数字，是用户交到我们手里的信任。它在币安的系统里被转走，责任就在币安。不在某一位工程师，不在某一项技术标准，责任就在我们。

钱，我们赔。账，大家可以在储备金证明页面自己查。被冻结和拦截的部分，我们会和执法部门、链上机构一起，一笔一笔追回来。

前两天，提币重新开放。那之后，我们所有的精力只放在一件事上，让每一笔提现都顺畅到账。这两天的提现规模，和被盗金额在同一个量级，每一笔我们都兑付了。用户的资产一直都在，我们没有挪用过用户的一分资产。

这是币安的底线。不要看我们说什么，但大家可以实实在在感受到我们做了什么！

报告发出去之前，内部也讨论过，哪些要讲，讲到什么程度，要不要说得好看一些。最后公司决策层定下来：不做任何修饰，所有事情如实向公众披露。

这是我们的文化，更是我们应尽的信任。说的和做的必须是一回事，绝不说一套、做一套。

我们很清楚，这份报告一发出去，一定会招来大量的质疑和批评。但这些声音是鞭策，也是让这个行业变得更安全的养分，我们全盘接受。所以我们把伤口摊开给大家看了。时间线、攻击路径、恶意脚本的每一步操作，连同我们自己没做好的地方，都写在里面。

为什么要把伤口摊开？因为这一刀，不只砍向币安。按 FBI 的通报，这是国家级的对手。今年以来，我们已经拦下 57 起疑似同一来源的攻击。他们敲的不只是我们这一扇门，把教训锁进抽屉，下一个受到影响的可能是任何一家。

道歉容易，但加固、改正更重要。报告里写到的入侵点，已经全部封堵。截至 11 月 3 日，受影响的钱包系统在全新环境里重建，内部 AI 工具重建并收紧了权限，受影响的设备全部更换，相关凭证和令牌全部作废，全员设备做了一遍强化扫描，钱包风控和异常检测也加了码。大家热议的权限管理和安全机制，我们也在逐项升级。

但也有一些防线，只能修在看不见的地方。公开它，就是把地图交给下一个攻击者。我们自己说的，大家未必信，所以我们请了独立的第三方安全机构来审查，结论出来后，会向大家公开。

很多人问，为什么一台工作电脑能碰到那么多权限，为什么不多设几道防控。实际情况是，门锁、监控、保险柜，多方安全计算签名、提现风控、权限隔离，这些该有的设计都有，也一直在运转。但同时我们也看到，在 AI 时代，很多过去行之有效的安全措施，正在暴露出新的缺口。

这次站在门外的，是什么样的对手？他们有足够的耐心，前后潜伏了几个月，从假招聘、被篡改的开发工具，到零日恶意软件，再把我们的内部 AI 工具变成自己的跳板，一层一层往里走。这不是一台电脑、几个权限被攻破就能完成的事，是一场准备了很久的连续进攻。

说这些，不是为自己开脱。门没看好，就是我们的错。但大家需要知道，AI 时代的攻击，已经来到了这个强度。

对同行，我想多说几句。这几天，有同行提出交易所之间要联防，实时预警，追踪可疑资金，依法及时冻结，大额提现到陌生地址时多加一道验证。这些建议，我们赞同，而且愿意做第一个参与的人，也愿意把这次的攻击特征分享给任何一家交易所，包括我们的竞争对手。

我们虚心接收大家的批评，但安全不是一场看台上的比赛，没有谁能一直坐在看台上。就像同行自己说的，每家每月都在应对这样的攻击。今天站在风口上的是币安，明天可能是任何一家。在这件事上，整个行业是同一条船。

我们越来越觉得，这次的事情不只发生在币安身上，它是整个行业的一个拐点。AI 时代的安全该怎么做，交易所之间该怎么协作，这些问题谁都绕不过去。币安会拿出自己的力量，为行业做出我们的贡献。

我们的态度：认错，整改，接受批评。
所有的意见，全都收下，只要是中肯的，话说得再重，我们都会认真听、积极吸收、认真改。批评越具体，越像一份体检报告，对我们越有用。

最后，也想对个别同行说一句。团结两个字，我们听到了，也愿意相信。但如果一边喊着团结，一边借一场安全事件落井下石，做仇恨宣泄，同时还在水下操作很多见不得人的勾当，这是否名不正言不顺？口口声声专注于行业，但无时不刻行拉踩营销之实，这真的值得歌颂么？行业的进步，靠的是严谨、客观的讨论，而不是拉踩和攻击。这个行业从来都是水涨船高，踩着别人过河的人，河水迟早也会漫到自己脚下。

谢谢这几天支持和批评我们的每一个人！

text:
One of the most interesting opportunities for crypto adoption has absolutely nothing to do with crypto itself.

Hear me out as pokemon cards might be one of the best examples of this.

Look how big this industry has become while still operating in a pretty traditional way.

The trading card market is estimated at $9.2 billion in 2026

Pokémon is celebrating its 30th anniversary, Pokémon TCG Pocket reached 150 million downloads in its first year, and we recently saw a Pikachu Illustrator card sell for $16.5 million by Logan Paul

But as a big fan of the franchise I always look at how difficult it can still be to actually trade them.

Think about it too.

If you own an expensive Pokémon card and want to sell it, you have to find a buyer, prove the card is authentic, deal with grading, shipping, insurance and potentially wait weeks before everything is settled.

And if you’re buying, you’re basically trusting that the seller is sending you exactly what you paid for (this is scary af)

This is a market worth billions of dollars, yet its infrastructure is from 15 years ago.

Which brings me to @deadstock_app.

I know we’ve heard the RWA narrative a thousand times in crypto, and most of the conversation usually revolves around tokenized treasuries, real estate or institutional products.

All interesting, but honestly, not particularly exciting for the average person.

Now imagine applying the same technology to something millions of people already collect and genuinely care about.

Real Pokemon cards.
Actual physical, graded cards stored in a vault, with each one represented by a token on Arbitrum.

You can open digital packs, receive a card that’s backed 1:1 by a real collectible, trade it onchain or redeem it and have the physical card shipped to you.

Deadstock offers to buy cards back at 90% of their assessed fair market value.

They have an exclusive tokenization partnership with JTCC, Japan Trading Card Center, one of Japan’s largest online mystery pack services.

And we all know people already buy Pokemon cards.

You don’t need to invent that demand.

You need to make the experience of owning and trading those cards better.

As crypto users we always tried to convince users about blockchain technology benefits

Maybe the best approach is to take something people already love and build better infrastructure around it.

You can check what they’re building at @deadstock_app

In the last 14 days, nearly 30,000 tasks ran for over an hour on Agent Arena. Within that hour, the average model made 332 tool calls.

In these long-horizon tasks, the right model choice can cut the cost by up to 66%.

For long-running jobs, weighing cost against capability becomes critical: Claude Opus 5.5 still scores higher, but costs twice as much per hour of work.

text:
Models by @GoogleDeepMind scale better on cost than their rivals.

Gemini 4 Carbon is the prime example. As tasks get more demanding, every rival gets more expensive relative to Carbon.

For a typical task, GPT-6 Astra by @OpenAI costs 3.4× as much, Claude Opus 5.5 by @AnthropicAI costs 3.9× as much, and GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheaper option at about half of Carbon’s cost (0.54×).

Across the 5% most expensive sessions, Carbon’s position improves against all three. Opus edges up to 4.2×, Astra’s cost roughly doubles relative to Carbon, and Sol’s discount shrinks.

This in turn can translate into meaningful savings across real-world tasks such as building an Android security app, one of many long-horizon tasks that our Agent Arena users delegate to their agents.
author: arena

As tasks get more complex, @GoogleDeepMind and @XiaomiMiMo are the biggest winners in the Agent Arena.

On cheaper tasks, @OpenAI and @AnthropicAI hold 10 of the 11 frontier spots. On the most expensive 5% of sessions, they hold just 7. The freed spots go to Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6 Flash and Pro.

These shifts matter as sessions costing $100 or more are not uncommon across real-world use cases coming from Agent Arena. Even within the last 2 weeks, more than 1,000 sessions crossed that boundary, and choosing a suboptimal model might have had a meaningful impact on that final bill.

They're called “zombie” (senescent) cells. They pile up and inflame the tissue around them which is bad for you body. 

This research group figured out how to kill them in mice. 

They found that these zombie cells run low on one fatty acid: DGLA. So they added it back causing many of the 
zombie cells to die while the healthy cells survived. 

They died by ferroptosis where the cell’s outer membrane oxidizes and breaks.

Would be interesting if replicated in humans.

A quick note on fully diluted vs. total basic share count:

Our pre-IPO perps are priced on fully diluted share count, and that won’t change at IPO.

Before an IPO, headline valuations are typically quoted on a fully diluted basis. After IPO, “market cap” is normally reported on total basic shares, which is a different number

So if a pre-IPO perp trades on fully diluted valuations but converts to basic shares at IPO, traders are forced to eat an adjustment they didn't agree to when they entered the contract.

text:
As predicted Ai needs cryptography for verification. The need in a multi-tennant environment with hosted clouds & model routers, that need increases. People need to verify they're getting the model they're paying for & to prove to regulators what model/weighs theyre using as these models become the backbone for securoty & enterprise workflows in regualted insdustries.  ZKP was always in the card as the complimentary solution for AI when the service demands third party trust in the AI blackbox.
but note that ANthropic's need to prove inference differs from crypto's use of ZKP. crypto-native projects optimized for cheap on-chain verification, so they wanted small proofs and accepted slow provers. Anthropic optimized for off-chain auditors and regulators, so it accepted 19 MB proofs and got a fast prover. Anthropic chose STARKs that can generate proofs fast - A batch of 24 requests proves in about 223 s, which works out to about 110 tokens/s. Thats roughly 72x the GPU time of serving the same requests on vLLM.
That led them to adopt STARK proofs that are both quantum secure & GPU friendly.

But & there's a huge but -  what Anthropic is really proving to third parties is just that the model weights in the hash commitment, were what was run as an integer in response to a single prompt. There's not enough to prove what exact model was actually run, just that the weighs were what was committed. 
That implies there are pretty intuitive ways to game this - commit to a cheaper model with similar weighs, rewriting promptes selectively cheat on the rest of the traffic that's not being samples or proven, randomness selection can steer tokens within the error rate of the proof

text: An important read on Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and the political implications of Democratic Party control of the two companies.
author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
These comments deserve far more attention. The 18 year old conservatorship of $FNMA and $FMCC poses a long term risk to the housing market. @BillAckman highlighted these issues recently. He warned that leaving the GSEs in limbo leaves them vulnerable to inefficiency and political weaponization.

At the risk of going into too much detail here is a synopsis or his talking points and perhaps a few of my own:

Political Weaponization:  F2 have a very large war chest and an indefinite conservatorship leaves trillions of dollars in cash generating mortgage capacity under absolute bureaucratic control. A change in administration can instantly weaponize this control to push social and political agendas, shifting the GSEs from neutral market utilities to partisan tools.

Distorting credit allocations: When the federal government controls the flow of capital, mortgage access can be manipulated based on political favoritism rather than merit. It has been pointed out that using Fannie and Freddie to grant mortgages on highly favorable, non-economic terms creates massive structural instability.

The spectre of the GFC: This exact dynamic precipitated the original 2007–2008 financial crisis. Prior to the crash, HUD progressively raised affordable housing quotas for the GSEs, forcing them to absorb toxic, unqualified loans to satisfy political homeownership agendas. Keeping them in conservatorship preserves the exact mechanism that allowed that crisis to happen.

Spreads are historically wide: Currently, the spread between the 30 year mortgage rate and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is highly elevated; sitting near 215 to 217 basis points, well above the historical average of ~150 basis points. This massive gap heavily penalizes everyday homebuyers with higher borrowing costs. The fact that spreads are wider than before the GFC dispels the notion that conservatorship suppresses the spreads. An explicit line of credit backstop may be more effective.

Government overreach widens the gap: Policy interventions such as mandates that alter mortgage callability or complicate refinancing rules increase risk premiums for MBS investors. This added policy uncertainty drives up the yields investors demand, directly widening mortgage spreads. Separately, nonpecuniary aspects like eleveated rates/duration risk up this demand and have nothing to do with F2.

Privatization can actually remove uncertainty: Formalizing privatization, acknowledging the GSEs' massive capital buffers, and executing a structured exit would eliminate the "political risk premium" hanging over the MBS market. Restoring the GSEs to the private market under fixed capital guidelines is the most direct path to compressing today’s bloated spreads.

The bailout is repaid: The narrative that Fannie and Freddie are a liability to the taxpayer is completely false. While the government injected $191 billion during the crisis, the GSEs have paid back over $301 billion to the Treasury.

Unlocking 100s of billions in value: Rather than a rushed IPO that risks destabilizing the market, the administration can immediately exercise its warrants for a 79.9% common stock stake (Subject to the SPS/LP repayment stated above) and relist the companies on the New York Stock Exchange. This "walk before you run" strategy would safely remove roughly $8 trillion in liabilities from the federal balance sheet while netting taxpayers a massive "mark-to-market" windfall.

text:
David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, has tracked 147 AI assistants so far, and in his group chats of AI power users, the number one fear is trust. It comes up in 22% of roughly 3,600 messages.

He puts agents through head-to-head tests, like ordering same-day flowers as cheaply as possible or planning a weekend in LA that's both luxurious and cost-efficient, to see which ones can hold competing preferences.

He joins a16z's Anish Acharya and Josh Elman to discuss why the scariest agent failures are the embarrassing ones, why agents are where e-commerce was in 1997, why scale is still a moat, and the "dark agent" that could speak to the parts of ourselves we don't reveal.

author: togethercompute
quoted_text:
Introducing the Together Compiler: continual compilation for AI inference! I’m super proud to finally share this work from our research team! ✨

Today’s inference is “Polymorphic” or shape-shifting, it doesn’t sit still. On OpenRouter, 80% of traffic goes to models released in the last three months and the top ten most popular open models each use a different architecture. Our customers constantly change their usage behaviors. Together Compiler leverages agents to continually optimize our deployments immediately as these changes occur.

Together Compiler research highlights include:
1. 252x better throughput: TKCC lets agents try 252x more optimization experiments per hour compared to prior agent inference optimization systems.
2. State-of-the-art TPS across InferenceX workloads we tried: TKCC outperforms the best InferenceX engine across all tested settings in just 24 hours & 2 nodes per compile. Including 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1 B200 and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash GB300 at batch size 1. NVIDIA, AMD, Trainium2.
3. Continuous recompilation: TKCC currently serves many trillions of production tokens per day and adapts to traffic shifts within just a few hours of recompilation.
4. Bitter lessons: TKCC’s design builds on 2+ years of building frameworks to accelerate AI Inference, starting from ThunderKittens and Megakernels. Compilers have always used abstractions and IRs, but we show that agentic compilers now reach higher performance ceilings without abstractions.

From an incredible team @reyna_abhyankar @dylan__lim @realDanFu @togethercompute!!

text:
For companies like $SIVE / $AAOI, the demand imbalance for lasers are so severe

That even a 20-30% overall demand reduction from a hypothetical DC slowdown would likely not eliminate the shortage. 

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

And obviously haircut growth valuations (but not to the point where demand collapses to 0).

Yet we're seeing everything in AI trade is getting lumped up together as something that requires heavy financing + not profitable.

text:
Legal engineering is one of my favourite parts about being a crypto lawyer. But I’ve become a bit jaded recently bc I realise it’s often a lot of theory crafting and mental masturbation simply due to the fact that enforcement has not been solved.

It’s not really a legal problem anymore, it’s an adverse selection problem combined with a free rider problem. 

Enshrining token holder protections via a memberless foundation or association has been done for years. MetaDAO or the handful of capital formation platforms that use a Cayman Fdn + SPC structure to commoditise the offshore governance structure isn’t creating a new legal unlock, albeit it is making these legal protections far more accessible at a fraction of the cost which is in itself a valuable offering. 

The unsolved issue isn’t whether or not we can create our own set of “rules” to govern the token. We can and we have.

The issue has always been twofold.

First, who wants to play the role of the policeman and the public prosecutor? The role of a policeman is thankless. The public prosecutor is friendless by design. Both must be funded by the public purse - which does not exist in our industry. 

So you could have the best legal protections on paper and you would do nothing if they were breached because the team wields immense commercial influence over the foundation structure which protects your rights or in the case of a capital formation platform, the platform has to sue its own founders which is commercially a non starter. 

The alternative of course is that you try and enforce your rights yourself which is again, not viable. If you held 1m worth of a 100m market cap token and your rights were infringed, lawyering up would cost you 50-100k to even get an initial view. Actually taking action would cost you a couple hundred grand in the first phase, and you would likely be dragged into arbitration in the islands. You will burn a million in the first year trying to enforce your rights against the structure that supposedly granted it because the powers that be don’t really want you to. Don't get me started on the fact that all your lawyers would likely be commercially conflicted, if not actually conflicted from acting for you, due to the legal / governance / structuring / professional services cabals which all cross-refer work and scratch each others' backs. 

Second, founders don't really like a structure that actually has real bite. And honestly why would they? Laws are created to protect those who are not in a position to protect themselves - it is difficult to find founders who are willing to spend time and effort on handcuffing themselves and limiting their options. Just because you don't intend to commit crime doesn't mean you would personally fund a policeman to surveil you 24/7 - that's unfortunately just not how incentives work. This means that the creation of these  legal structures is often an attempt by founders to borrow legitimacy from lawyers or incumbent launchpads for marketing purposes in order to fill a fundraise. 

Rights without anyone to enforce the rights are worthless.

I'm not knocking on the work Gabe has done, or MetaDAO or any of the other actors (including myself) looking to bring the space forward. Don't get me wrong, good legal structuring is a step in the right direction and its an important one.

It just makes me feel a bit like Cassandra knowing that something has to break massively before we realize that legal and enforcement has to be designed ab initio as a public good - and even longer for us to realize that public goods require public funding - and even longer to figure out a workable mechanism for taxation. 

I think we will get there though but this is likely a decades long initiative. Kind of just ranting because I'm impatient I suppose.

yeah this is an overly simplified view ser 

how many contract disputes get to litigation? 

but what the contracts say is not meaningless just because it never got litigated, it affects the game theory & economics of a settlement negotiation

I can tell you I've already seen this play out in many situations where we put in place these types of tokenholder protections...getting much better outcomes for investors than if they had just signed a ridiculous Cayman-style no-strings-attached SAFT that is close to being an illusory promise....these types of outcomes are also "enforcement of rights" even though it's a pre-litigation settlement in effect 

contracts and duties also do affect how founders behave in general...how often do officers of DE corps get successfully sued for breach of fiduciary duty? but they do know they have duties and this leads to convos with lawyers which often persuades them not to do dumb shit, again without any "enforcemetn" ever having happened, but with the rules and agreements mattering....

when combined with smart contract mechs that also give leverage to investors, all the better/more effective as well. . . 

so it's not just theoretically sound, it's practical...in fact I'd probably say it's more practically oriented than theoretical in general

Last night was special.

Election days just never get old for us at Polymarket. Watching regular people experience the beauty of market based forecasts as the results come in. How practically useful it is. How simple it is to interpret. When it clicks, it clicks.

It’s now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks. The networks hold out until absolute certainty, and the suspense keeps it entertaining all night. No knock to them, but now there’s Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what's happening in real time.

I know the industry has gained a mixed rap for a variety of reasons, many of which are criticisms with real merit. But I think I speak for both myself and my peers when I say we got into this because we really love the idea of markets being able to place a price on the future (e.g. Democrats had a 92% chance to take the House on Polymarket), and how that can help people better understand what's likely to happen and make decisions accordingly.

Our mission is to make sure we deliver on the promise of prediction markets, which was on full display last night. In the midst of so much noise around what we do, the American people get to see what Polymarket is really all about. Feels like one step closer to the dream. Onwards.

A new identity. A broader vision. Energy Forever, For All.

SECI has introduced its new logo at Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo (BRESE) 2026, marking an important milestone in the organisation’s journey as it continues to expand its role across India’s renewable energy landscape.

The new logo represents energy in continuous motion - renewable, regenerative and forward-moving. Its rotating forms, inspired by turbine blades, symbolise the expansion of India’s renewable energy infrastructure. At its centre, the embedded Vajra represents power and activation, while the surrounding vortex of leaves signifies a continuous, self-sustaining cycle of renewable energy. The six elements of the design represent the sky, earth and the four directions, reflecting SECI’s reach and leadership across the renewable energy landscape.

The colour palette reinforces this vision: Blue conveys institutional trust, technical expertise and leadership; Green represents regeneration, sustainability and India’s commitment to a clean energy future; while Sunrise Saffron symbolises the dawn of India’s renewable energy revolution, with SECI leading innovation towards a sustainable future.

Designed by the National Institute of Design (NID), Ahmedabad, through a consultative process with SECI, the new visual identity reflects the organisation’s evolution beyond its solar origins into an integrated renewable energy organisation, with a growing presence across solar, wind, hybrid energy, energy storage, green hydrogen and its derivatives.

SECI - Energy Forever, For All.

quoted_text:
🔴 Fraude chez Crédit Mutuel Arkéa (@cmarkea) : la banque sort du silence et détaille l'attaque

Le groupe a fini par publier un communiqué ce mercredi à 18h10.

Voici ce qu'il faut en retenir.

👉 Le mode opératoire

Selon la banque, les attaquants se sont servis du compte propre de Crédit Mutuel Arkéa. Depuis ce compte, ils ont réalisé des transactions vers d'autres établissements bancaires, et les fonds auraient ensuite été convertis en cryptos sur des plateformes spécialisées.

C'est par la plateforme d'un prestataire du groupe que l'accès aurait été obtenu, ce qui a permis aux attaquants d'atteindre Arkéa directement. Son nom n'a pas été communiqué.

Pas d'erreur humaine en interne, assure la banque. Elle parle d'une "attaque sophistiquée venant de l'extérieur", désormais "circonscrite".

👉 Fortuneo

J'ai rapporté, après l'analyse de plusieurs sources, que les fonds seraient sortis via sa filiale Fortuneo.

La banque dément quant à elle que "l'entrée" des pirates se soit faite par sa filiale.

Elle indique aussi que c'est le compte propre de Crédit Mutuel Arkéa qui a été ponctionné.

Il y a encore des zones d'ombre à ce niveau.

👉 L'ampleur des dégâts

Interrogée sur le chiffre de 118 millions d'euros (133 millions de dollars), la banque ne le confirme pas mais en "valide l'ordre de grandeur". Une partie des fonds a pu être bloquée. Des actions de recouvrement sont en cours.

Ces montants ne sont "absolument pas de nature à remettre en cause" sa solidité financière, assure le groupe, dont le total de bilan atteint, pour mémoire, 211,5 milliards d'euros.

👉 Les clients

Côté clients, aucune conséquence sur les avoirs, toujours d'après la banque. L'incident s'est seulement traduit par l'exécution différée de certains virements, la plupart des opérations ayant repris dans la matinée. Mais le groupe les appelle quand même à la vigilance face à une possible recrudescence des tentatives de phishing.

👉 Les autorités

Le groupe dit avoir informé les autorités de supervision. Il travaille aussi avec les autorités judiciaires et policières pour établir l'origine de l'attaque.

👉 Ce qui reste flou

La banque affirme avoir identifié "très rapidement" les activités suspectes. Or les premiers retraits onchain remontent au 1er novembre, et @zachxbt estime que plus de 30 millions de dollars auraient pu être gelés avec une déclaration plus rapide.

Restent plusieurs points à éclaircir.

Qui est ce prestataire ? À quelle date exacte l'attaque a-t-elle été détectée, et quand les superviseurs ont-ils été notifiés ? Et comment des virements de cette ampleur ont-ils pu partir du compte propre de la banque ?

À suivre.

Pendle splits yield from principal, and pETH splits into its floor (fpETH) and its premium (vpETH).

The floor would just grow with no risk of losing value in ETH terms.

And then you'd have your vpETH, which would be exposed to spot price volatility, so you can trade it or just sell it to get a low-volatility position.

Introducing the Together Compiler: continual compilation for AI inference! I’m super proud to finally share this work from our research team! ✨

Today’s inference is “Polymorphic” or shape-shifting, it doesn’t sit still. On OpenRouter, 80% of traffic goes to models released in the last three months and the top ten most popular open models each use a different architecture. Our customers constantly change their usage behaviors. Together Compiler leverages agents to continually optimize our deployments immediately as these changes occur.

Together Compiler research highlights include:
1. 252x better throughput: TKCC lets agents try 252x more optimization experiments per hour compared to prior agent inference optimization systems.
2. State-of-the-art TPS across InferenceX workloads we tried: TKCC outperforms the best InferenceX engine across all tested settings in just 24 hours & 2 nodes per compile. Including 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1 B200 and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash GB300 at batch size 1. NVIDIA, AMD, Trainium2.
3. Continuous recompilation: TKCC currently serves many trillions of production tokens per day and adapts to traffic shifts within just a few hours of recompilation.
4. Bitter lessons: TKCC’s design builds on 2+ years of building frameworks to accelerate AI Inference, starting from ThunderKittens and Megakernels. Compilers have always used abstractions and IRs, but we show that agentic compilers now reach higher performance ceilings without abstractions.

From an incredible team @reyna_abhyankar @dylan__lim @realDanFu @togethercompute!!

text:
Coinbase's Stand With Crypto may have rated Sherrod Brown an F, but they also sponsored the US Army...

If what brought you to crypto was CROPS and "don't trust, verify," I would wager your views are closer to Sherrod Brown's than you think.

Brown has had nuanced views of crypto and a keen sense of what his constituents need. Winning him over is worth more than demonizing him.

He voted against the PATRIOT Act in 2001, when only 66 House members did, and he has voted against nearly every expansion of government surveillance since, from the Bush-era wiretapping bills to Section 702, where in 2024 he voted to require a warrant before the government could read Americans' communications swept up by it. In his words, "Privacy is a civil right," and "When you sign away your privacy rights to a corporation, you've basically given the government permission to sift through your secrets as well."

He's also understood why people come to crypto for a long time. On bitcoin's tenth anniversary in 2018, he said "you can't blame some Americans for hoping that an alternative banking system could be created that would be superior to the one in shambles at that time," and that he hoped it would help "people who are unbanked or underserved by the traditional financial system."

His biggest problem has been corporations controlling people's money. In 2019 he fought Facebook's Libra, a permissioned coin from a company fresh off the Cambridge Analytica scandal, and in 2021 he called out stablecoins for the same thing: "It is not decentralized when one company controls when people can access their own money." That same week he said "my job is not to resist or say no to cryptocurrency generally." He did push for a CBDC, first proposed in 2020 so people could get COVID relief without paying check cashers, but he insisted it "maintains individual privacy" and "operates side-by-side with cash." I can't find him pushing it since 2022.

Then FTX defrauded its customers. In 2022 he said he couldn't see anything useful about hundreds of speculative cryptocurrencies, and when asked about banning crypto, he said a ban would be "very difficult because it will go offshore."

Colleagues like Elizabeth Warren pushed bank-style KYC onto wallets, miners and validators. Brown went after the companies that actually held customer money, pushing for real disclosures, separate customer funds and limits on insider conflicts. He even flagged token disclosures that "fail to align with the software code behind a token." As he put it, "It is far easier to profit when customers are left in the dark." Even then, he told a room of bankers, "We know why crypto and fintechs are appealing to people... People are fed up with fees on everything."

By 2024 he was saying "I'm not automatically saying no" to crypto legislation, and wanted to pair a stablecoin bill with banking access for legal cannabis businesses and clawbacks of pay from failed-bank executives. Ending debanking and holding bankers accountable is the fight crypto was born in. In 2025 he called cryptocurrency "a part of America's economy" and said his goal was making sure it "expands opportunity and lifts up Ohioans."

Voting him out didn't fix everything. Roman Storm was still convicted, and Trump's own US attorney defended the verdict.

Supporters raised more than $5 million for Storm's legal defense. The industry spent more than $100 million across the 2024 and 2026 races trying to beat Brown, and he's back in the Senate anyway. I would have much rather seen that money go toward Storm's defense, or something like the Coinbase-backed lawsuit that got Tornado Cash's sanctions ruled unlawful, or anything else that produced results aligned with CROPS.

Brown is a reasonable man who has proven willing to change his mind. There's a real opportunity to align incentives with him around protecting Ohioans while promoting self-custody, DeFi, and CROPS values.

quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

Last night was special.

Election days just never get old for us at Polymarket. Watching regular people experience the beauty of market based forecasts as the results come in. How practically useful it is. How simple it is to interpret. When it clicks, it clicks.

It’s now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks. The networks hold out until absolute certainty, and the suspense keeps it entertaining all night. No knock to them, but now there’s Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what's happening in real time.

I know the industry has gained a mixed rap for a variety of reasons, many of which are criticisms with real merit. But I think I speak for both myself and my peers when I say we got into this because we really love the idea of markets being able to place a price on the future (e.g. Democrats had a 92% chance to take the House on Polymarket), and how that can help people better understand what's likely to happen and make decisions accordingly.

Our mission is to make sure we deliver on the promise of prediction markets, which was on full display last night. In the midst of so much noise around what we do, the American people get to see what Polymarket is really all about. Feels like one step closer to the dream. Onwards.

Global fund flows: ex-US rebounding, crypto the lone laggard

Fund flow momentum is rotating. US equities are weakening on a flow basis while ex-US is picking back up, with developed markets moderating and emerging markets improving. That's the top-level read from RBC's latest flows work.

On the fixed income side, ex-US bond flows show stabilization with the 4-week average positive. Monthly ex-US equity flows are still positive, though the 4-week average is trending downward. So sustained demand, but losing a bit of steam on the shorter look.

Crypto is the only asset class sitting in the lagging quadrant, negative on both the weekly and 4-week average basis. Everything else in the global asset class universe, equities, bonds, money markets, is in positive flow territory. That's a clean contrast.

On sectors, Health Care/Biotech and Energy are in the "What's In" column. Consumer, Utilities, and Real Estate are out. Within thematics, AI, Cybersecurity, and Semiconductors have positive flows on both measures. Industrial Metals, Rare Earths, and Space and Satellite do not. In commodities, Brent crude flows improved, metals are fading, and gold is holding up despite a weekly demand slowdown.

Ethereum has always been many voices, hearts and minds: thousands of talks across conferences, meetups, workshops and podcasts, scattered across the internet. But decentralization does not have to mean fragmentation.

While decentralization is about power, fragmentation is about ecosystem amnesia: insights that are forgotten because nobody can find them, the same lessons learned over and over or newcomers starting from zero because the wisdom of those before them is buried somewhere they'll never look.

Ethereum got the first one right. But for too long we ignored the cost of the second.

Every builder who stood on stage and shared what they learned, every researcher who explained a hard idea and every core dev call where a protocol upgrade took shape all have given important gifts to the broader ecosystem.

These gifts deserve to be cherished, remembered and more importantly, discovered. Because ultimately, a movement that forgets its own history slowly loses its soul.

That's why I'm sooo happy to see Ethereum TV come to life as a searchable memory of the Ethereum ecosystem, unifying the invaluable collective knowledge and wisdom we've built together over the years!

Ethereum TV began as an idea I couldn't let go of, but many ideas stay just ideas. Very few get to become real. And even fewer ideas find the right people. Seeing this one come to life, carried by people who believed in it as much as I did, is pure magic.

Now it belongs to all of us. Thank you @ethereumtv_ ! ❤️

text: Important to understand that pre IPO valuation and post IPO valuation are calculated differently. Consistency across regimes is crucial for pre-IPO instruments to stay fair.
author: meower888
quoted_text:
A quick note on fully diluted vs. total basic share count:

Our pre-IPO perps are priced on fully diluted share count, and that won’t change at IPO.

Before an IPO, headline valuations are typically quoted on a fully diluted basis. After IPO, “market cap” is normally reported on total basic shares, which is a different number

So if a pre-IPO perp trades on fully diluted valuations but converts to basic shares at IPO, traders are forced to eat an adjustment they didn't agree to when they entered the contract.

text:
My wife and I had a son 5 months ago. 

We were both uncertain if we wanted him.

Why? We really enjoyed our life and the fear of a new variable disrupting that was very scary.  

And the first 2 months into it, we were still uncertain. It felt more like a nuisance than a benefit.

We also lived a life of extremes. Each with 120+ nights per year in a hotel, hiking every weekend, racing cars and a ton of solo time. The relative change was real. 

There's a mourning of your old life.

But then the postpartum hormonal extravaganza ends, you settle into the change and adapt to the new. 

You realize how incredibly special a child is. 

It's difficult to explain until you have one, but I liken it to the gut punch feeling and chemistry you experience with a first love. There's a draw to that person that is more important to you than anything else. And the weirdest part is no one else feels this same yearning.

If you don't have a kid, this might also help you understand how looking at your kid is way different than looking at someone else's... because I really don't care for anyone else's. 

But mine? When I'm away for more than 4 hours I catch myself smiling at a photo of him and anxiously anticipating when I get to see him again

You solidify the family unit. And imagine a future together that's much greater than "happy".

Then there's a wonderful realization you can still thread in the parts of your old life that mattered.

Prioritization becomes clear. 

My wife and I learned how to work even better together for each other, ourselves and the family.

Could we have been fine without kids? Probably. We're pretty adaptable as humans. 

But does the good outweigh the bad and is that worth taking a chance on the regret index? Absolutely. 100x.

It's difficult to explain, but I suppose anything encoded into us over millions of years is.

text:
以前玩合约，我基本只考虑两个问题：涨还是跌，开多少倍。

后来慢慢接触美股，发现期权其实挺有意思的

比如我看好英伟达接下来一个月的走势，但又不想直接买入股票，就可以考虑买入看涨期权。

提前付一笔权利金，如果后面涨幅足够大，就有机会赚钱。如果判断错了，作为期权买方，最多损失这笔权利金。

当然，期权有个很容易踩的坑。

不是你看对方向就一定赚钱，还得看涨多少、什么时候涨。哪怕英伟达真的涨了，涨幅不够覆盖成本，到期一样可能亏钱。

最近 OKX 推出了简易期权，我比较喜欢的一点是，它把原本复杂的期权交易做得更直观了。

一股对应的期权名义数量就能起步，7×24 小时可以询价，下单前还能看到权利金、盈亏平衡价这些关键数据。

我觉得对于我们这些习惯了现货和永续的币圈玩家来说，期权确实值得花点时间研究。

毕竟交易不只有做多和做空，有时候换一种工具，整个交易思路都会不一样。
author: youyou5202
quoted_text:
昨天简单的带大家看了看我们弹出的期权页面，但是评论区还是很多朋友头大，毕竟第一次研究Call、Put、Buy、Sell…

跟着OKX来试试，小白也可以轻松上手～ 

🌟我们只要先问自己四个问题。

看好上涨，想用较少资金参与？

看跌，或想给持仓加一层保护？

已经持有，想多收一笔权利金？

想买，但只愿意接受某个价格？

这四个问题，正好对应 OKX 简易期权的四种玩法，大师的玩法，也能简单上手，我们接着往下看。 

🌟我们先理解一下期权到底是什么？

把期权理解成一份有期限的约定，买方付出一笔权利金，获得一项权利。

卖方收取权利金，同时承担履约义务。

说得再直白一点：

买方先付钱，买一个未来的选择。
卖方先收钱，答应满足条件时履约。

注意，权利金不是稳赚的利息，而是对风险和义务的交换。

🌟四种玩法，一起来看看。

⑴认为会涨：买入看涨

支付权利金，用较少资金参与上涨。

但不是涨了就一定赚，上涨幅度还要覆盖权利金。

最大亏损为已经支付的权利金。

⑵认为会跌：买入看跌

价格跌得足够多，期权才可能产生收益。

如果已经持有相应资产，也可以搭配买入看跌期权，为持仓增加一层保护。

但保护有成本，也有期限，不能消除所有亏损。

⑶已有持仓：卖出看涨

用持仓作担保，先收一笔权利金。

如果到期价格没有超过行权价，可以继续持有，收到的权利金也会保留。

如果到期价格达到或超过行权价，就需要按照行权价卖出。

代价是，如果价格大涨，你会让出行权价以上的涨幅。

⑷计划买入：卖出看跌

先确定一个自己愿意接受的买入价，再收取权利金。

如果到期价格高于行权价，不需要买入，收到的权利金仍然保留。

如果到期价格不高于行权价，就需要按照行权价买入，收到的权利金同样保留。

但如果价格大幅下跌，也必须按照约定履约，损失可能远远超过收到的权利金。

🌟在 OKX 操作指南

打开 OKX 首页，依次进入交易、期权、简易期权。

第一步，选择想参与的标的。

第二步，选择上涨、下跌、持仓增收或计划买入。

第三步，选择到期日和行权价。

第四步，查看权利金、盈亏平衡价和可能的结果。

第五步，确认自己能够接受最坏结果，再决定是否下单。

在OKX玩简单期权，好就好在不用先学会看复杂的期权链，也不用自己计算所有结果。

🌟它简单在哪里？

OKX 简易期权目前支持部分代币化股票期权。

支持买入看涨、买入看跌、卖出看涨和卖出看跌四种基础玩法。

7x24H均可询价交易，可以按照一股对应的期权名义数量起步。

下单前可以查看成本、盈亏平衡价和可能的结果。

不另外收取交易手续费，但相关成本已经体现在报价价差中。

（具体支持范围和可用报价以产品页面显示为准）

不过呀，操作变简单，不代表风险变小，买方可能损失全部权利金，卖方需要备足担保，并承担到期履约义务。

即使方向判断正确，也可能因为涨跌幅度不够或剩余时间不足而亏损。

所以使用期权前，不要只问能赚多少，还要问自己，最坏会发生什么，我能不能接受？

最后，我自己有个习惯，无论用不用，但是我看到什么学什么，先把知识储备起来，因为我相信多学点东西没坏处，和Misa一起来学习简易期权吧😎🖤

After Google acquired my AR startup, I started thinking about the next interface, this time for AI. Text and voice work fine, just like DOS did before the Mac. But nothing’s more intuitive than face to face.

After two years of research, today we’re launching Atmee v2: a real-time avatar model that makes live video agents feel truly life-like.

• Any character from 1 image + 10s of audio
• Contextual expressions, gestures, even interacting with the environment
• Live video calls, voice only, or video generation

At its core, Atmee v2 is a video foundation model, it can render anything, but it’s built to excel at characters, which is what video models like Seedance 2.5 and Wan 3.0 are mostly used for. In comparison:
Atmee v2

• Up to 50x faster
• 10-100x cheaper

Build tutors, sales coaches, support agents, companions, game characters, even whole living worlds. The interface after text and voice starts today.

author: togethercompute
quoted_text:
Introducing the Together Compiler: continual compilation for AI inference! I’m super proud to finally share this work from our research team! ✨

Today’s inference is “Polymorphic” or shape-shifting, it doesn’t sit still. On OpenRouter, 80% of traffic goes to models released in the last three months and the top ten most popular open models each use a different architecture. Our customers constantly change their usage behaviors. Together Compiler leverages agents to continually optimize our deployments immediately as these changes occur.

Together Compiler research highlights include:
1. 252x better throughput: TKCC lets agents try 252x more optimization experiments per hour compared to prior agent inference optimization systems.
2. State-of-the-art TPS across InferenceX workloads we tried: TKCC outperforms the best InferenceX engine across all tested settings in just 24 hours & 2 nodes per compile. Including 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1 B200 and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash GB300 at batch size 1. NVIDIA, AMD, Trainium2.
3. Continuous recompilation: TKCC currently serves many trillions of production tokens per day and adapts to traffic shifts within just a few hours of recompilation.
4. Bitter lessons: TKCC’s design builds on 2+ years of building frameworks to accelerate AI Inference, starting from ThunderKittens and Megakernels. Compilers have always used abstractions and IRs, but we show that agentic compilers now reach higher performance ceilings without abstractions.

From an incredible team @reyna_abhyankar @dylan__lim @realDanFu @togethercompute!!

author: CryptoScoopOG
quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

text:
My brutally honest advice to someone who wants to make a lot of money.

3 things nobody told you:

1. The only way to make a lot of money is to create a lot of value.

No one hands out money. No one is going to pay you just because they like you or think you're cool.

Money earned is a direct byproduct of value created.

The only way to get rich is to create an enormous amount of value for others, and capture a small portion of that along the way.

You create value by doing three things:

- Identify problems
- Create solutions
- Scale those solutions

It's not talking about the thing, it's not brainstorming about the thing, it's not asking about the thing, it's not thinking about the thing. The only way to create value is by doing the thing.

And if you don't know where to start, look around you. Customers, colleagues, bosses, shareholders, employees. Every single one of them has a problem.

What problems can you solve for the people around you?

Figure them out, solve them, scale that solution.

That's how you make money.

2. You don't need passion, you need energy.

I still have no idea what it means to follow your passion.

You don't have to be passionate about your professional pursuits, you just need to find energy in them. You just need to feel a pull towards them. You just need to feel that spark of curiosity in them.

Passion is usually a byproduct of energy.

When you have energy for something, you'll give it your deep attention to learn more.

You’ll ask the right questions. You’ll figure it out. You’ll win.

Follow your energy. Pursue interesting puzzles. Solve them.

3. You have to demonstrate excellence in everything you do.

Your income scales proportional to the amount of excellence that you're able to demonstrate.

Strategic incompetence is a lie. You don't get to pick and choose when to show up, because the world will ignore your best and judge you for your worst. Everything matters. Every single thing.

Top performers show up with energy and enthusiasm for the little things just as much as they do for the big things.

If you're in the top-10% of performers, there's no ceiling for what you can do. But the self-awareness to identify where you currently stack up, and adapt to the honest feedback on it, is very rare.

If you're in the top-10%, you know it. If you're not, figure out why and fix it.

quoted_text:
After DOGE, Elon came to a conclusion most people missed.

He tried to reform the state from the inside. He failed. And he said it plainly: the government can't fix its own deficit. Nobody in power actually wants to cut. The machine protects itself.

So he drew the only logical conclusion. If the state can't be reformed, there are only two ways this ends.

Either global bankruptcy. Debt keeps compounding, interest payments eat the budget, and the system collapses under its own weight.

Or robots. AI and robotics grow the economy so fast that the debt becomes manageable, and abundance makes the old fights over scarcity irrelevant.

Here's the part almost nobody sees.

For two centuries, capitalism has had a marketing problem. Its gains are real but slow and invisible. 2% growth a year doesn't feel like anything. Your life gets better over 30 years and you never connect it to the system that did it. Meanwhile, the left's promises feel immediate and concrete: a check, a subsidy, a benefit. That's why the left wins on promises even when it can't deliver them. Capitalism produces the wealth, socialism takes the credit.

Robots break that asymmetry.

When productivity doubles in a few years instead of a few decades, people will see it. Things get cheaper, services get better, opportunities appear, in real time. For the first time in history, people will connect capitalism and their rising standard of living directly, almost instantly. The causal chain becomes visible.

And that changes everything politically.

So there are two scenarios.

Scenario one: we stay in the current inertia. No breakthrough, or a breakthrough we regulate to death. The debt wins. Living standards stagnate, then fall. A frustrated electorate turns to whoever promises the most, and that pushes toward a hard collectivist left. But collectivism fails, as it always does. And when it fails, the most organized, most disciplined collectivist force left standing isn't the old left. It's radical Islamism. Bankruptcy, then communism, then something worse.

Scenario two: robots win. Abundance arrives, and it arrives visibly. The link between free enterprise and prosperity becomes obvious to everyone. And this is the key point: it becomes obvious to everyone, including the minorities the left was counting on. Because their long-term incentive is the same as everyone else's. A kid in the suburbs gains infinitely more from a booming, abundant West than from a bankrupt state handing out promises it can't keep. Abundance is the most powerful integration machine ever built.

That's the Western renaissance.

The West doesn't need to win the culture war by arguing. It needs to win it by delivering. And for the first time, it has the technology to deliver fast enough for people to notice.

The race isn't left vs right anymore. It's robots vs bankruptcy.

🇭🇰 在 Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 期間，由新火集團聯合 @BitGo主辦的閉門酒會「The Principals' Evening」於昨晚在港圓滿落幕！

酒會現場，新火集團 CEO 翁曉奇重磅宣佈：新火集團正籌備推出「新火全球宏觀多資產策略」，目前已正式進入種子資金試運行階段。🚀

💡 【FICC+C】獨家投研框架：由新火集團首席經濟學家付鵬主導構建，為該策略注入頂級宏觀策略洞察。其中，FICC通常指固定收益（Fixed Income，含利率研究）、外匯（Currencies）、大宗商品（Commodities）及權益類資產；在本策略框架下，利率被作為獨立宏觀變數重點跟蹤；“+C”則指向數字資產（Crypto/Digital Assets）及權益類資產。

📝 一句話總結：FICC+C 策略，就是以“全球資金成本（FI）、匯率天平（C）、大宗商品實體供需（C）”、加密資產（+C）和權益類資產為交易對象，捕捉全球宏觀大齒輪咬合過程中的價格偏差以及趨勢性機會。

付鵬先生自2026年4月加入新火集團以來，便持續參與集團宏觀研究、資產配置框架及產品化方向的建設。數月時間內，付鵬先生圍繞全球利率、通脹、美元、流動性、匯率及風險偏好等主題，持續推進宏觀投研體系建設，並多次在集團內分享對全球經濟、金融市場和數字資產發展的觀察與思考。

新火集團首席執行官翁曉奇表示：“‘新火全球宏觀多資產策略’是新火集團在資產管理方向上的重要探索。它不只是增加一項產品，更代表新火集團希望從數字資產服務，進一步延伸至研究驅動的多資產配置和長期資產管理服務。”

quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

author: CryptoScoopOG
quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

text:
King of the Markets has officially concluded.

KotM was built to pilot and prove out the Reserve's liquidity thesis, and the results have surpassed all expectations. A more detailed breakdown of the data will be released this week, but for now, some important information regarding rewards.

1) A big part of this process is making sure the reward pool isn't being diluted by sybils and people who tried to game the system (wash traders and token ruggers) so we're taking the time to review all the data before distributing anything.

We've already begun filtering through transaction data to identify wash trading and accounts that attempted to artificially farm points. We want to make sure rewards go to legitimate traders and deployers, not those who tried to game the system.

2) In approximately 6.5 hours, the KotM page will update to show your trading and launchpad activity. You'll be asked to sign with your wallet to confirm where you'd like to receive your rewards and in which token. This is completely free, requires no gas, and takes about 5 seconds.

3) You'll have 120 hours (5 days) to complete this step. If you don't sign within that window, you will not be eligible to receive rewards. Once the 120 hours are up, we'll run one final filter and redistribute any unclaimed rewards from wallets that didn't sign among eligible wallets that did.

4) For those who traded through FOMO, unfortunately, FOMO doesn't make its wallet API public, which makes tracking your activity extremely difficult. We still want to make sure FOMO users aren't left out of rewards, so the best solution we have for now is to export your EVM private key from FOMO and import it into a compatible wallet.

From there, check the FOMO box and complete your payout confirmation, even if your stats show zero activity. We'll manually review these wallets over the coming days to make sure legitimate activity is accounted for.

Please only import your private key into a trusted wallet app. Never share it with anyone or enter it on the KotM website.

5) Once the final filtering and redistribution are complete, rewards will be airdropped directly to your specified wallet in your selected currency.

We appreciate everyone who participated in the pilot. The results have given us a lot of confidence in what we're building, and there's much more to come.

text:
i asked Amjad Masad, the founder of Replit, why he thinks someone who started vibe coding 3 months ago might be better than someone who started 3 years ago.

my takeaway? some engineers have spent 3 years getting better at asking AI to do less.
🧵
1/ The problem is scar tissue.
And not knowing how to code might actually be an advantage.
People who started with early AI learned all the things it couldn't do.
So they built elaborate prompts, skill files, rules, and workarounds.
The models improved. Their habits didn't.
Amjad pointed out that even his own prompts have gotten lazier. Stronger models don't need the same micromanagement.
I've been thinking about the ambition cost of this. Not just the time wasted on unnecessary workarounds, but all the things we stop attempting because an older model convinced us they weren't possible.
2/ Here's where I disagree slightly.
Knowing how to code is an ENORMOUS advantage.
But only if you can resist the urge to micromanage implementation.
The best engineers should be able to delegate an entire outcome, recognize when the AI is wrong, and verify the result.
Their advantage isn't writing more code. It's knowing what good looks like for the use case.
3/ Now apply this to an entire engineering team.
Your models get smarter every few months.
But your company's knowledge? It gets buried in Slack, GitHub, old tickets, outdated docs, and decisions nobody remembers making.
So your agents inherit yesterday's assumptions, while your engineers keep repeating yesterday's explanations.
I wonder how much of the next leap in productivity comes from better models, and how much comes from finally questioning the limits we've gotten used to.
https://t.co/FqQ3XEljwY

author: IamRamenPanda
quoted_text:
昨晚，我的律师向法院提出动议，请求制裁世界自由金融(World Liberty Financial) @worldlibertyfi。理由是：它在我起诉它好几个月之后，才披露自己是阿联酋 🇦🇪 公民。

先给刚关注这场纠纷的朋友介绍一下：我是 World Liberty 最早、也是最大的投资人之一。2024 年 11 月，我和 World Liberty 签了代币购买协议，同意购买 3,000 万美元的WLFI代币，后来又把总投资增加到 4,500 万美元。

今年 4 月，我起诉了 World Liberty，指控这家公司用欺诈手段诱使我投资，之后又非法冻结了我的代币。

根据我的代币购买协议，我有权选择在加州的联邦法院或州法院提起诉讼。

我选了联邦法院。

像我这样的案子，只有在双方来自不同地方时，联邦法院才能审理。像我这样的外国原告，可以在联邦法院起诉美国被告，但一般不能在那里起诉外国被告。在这个问题上，像 World Liberty 这样的公司，会被视为拥有它每一个所有者的公民身份。所以只要有一个所有者是外国人，这家公司就算外国公司。

换句话说，只要 World Liberty 和它的所有者全都是美国人，我的案子就可以由联邦法院审理。

按照联邦法院的规则，World Liberty 必须在案件一开始就提交一份披露声明，列明它的每一个所有者，以及他们各自是哪里的公民。World Liberty 的披露声明只列了一个实体，就是 World Liberty 自己，公民身份只写了佛罗里达州。它的律师还签字证明，不知道还有其他需要披露的人。

随后，World Liberty 申请强制仲裁，想把我的案子从公开法庭转到秘密的仲裁程序中。

我反对这项申请。我的律师为此花了好几个月、几十万美元。在 8 月的一次听证会上，法院表示，它并不认为我的诉求都应该交付仲裁。法院裁定，我的部分诉求留在公开法庭审理，部分交付仲裁，并命令双方协商，拟定一份协议，划分哪些诉求留在法庭、哪些交付仲裁。

不到一周，World Liberty 突然"更正"了它的披露声明。之前它的所有权链条上只列了一个成员，现在列了 22 个，公民身份也变成了佛罗里达州、特拉华州、波多黎各和阿联酋。

World Liberty 现在说，联邦法院对我的案子没有管辖权，因为它有阿联酋公民身份，这样原告和被告双方就都有外国当事人。

这其中的讽刺显而易见。World Liberty 的"金皮书"宣称："World Liberty Financial 在设计上就不是在离岸注册的"，是"一家美国的、纳税的公司，致力于把 DeFi 带回它真正的家：美国"。它承诺打造一个"总部在美国的去中心化平台"，建立在"自由、隐私和交易自由的美国理念"之上，把不经中介的私人交易称为"美国的核心价值"，还夸口说："World Liberty Financial 不回避美国，而是拥抱美国，让它成为未来的全球加密之都。"

卖代币的时候，World Liberty 是骄傲的美国公司 🇺🇸。直到它需要想办法逃离美国联邦法庭的时候，才"发现"了自己的阿联酋 🇦🇪 血统。

World Liberty 想必一直都知道自己的所有者是谁。它的律师却声称，他们是在提交最初的披露声明之后，才得知公司有阿联酋公民身份。

正如我的动议所说，如果这是真的，那么要么是 World Liberty 的律师没有尽到应有的核查义务，要么是 World Liberty 没有对自己的律师说实话。我们问他们这是怎么回事，World Liberty 拒绝回答。

代币持有人有权知道，他们投资的项目对公众、对法院说的是不是真话。我提出这项动议，是要追究 World Liberty 及其律师的责任，因为我认为他们向法院提交了误导性的披露声明。我也要确保 World Liberty 耍手段的代价由他们自己承担，而不是由我承担。

联邦法院对这项制裁动议作出裁决后，我会在加州州法院重新起诉 World Liberty。

我会继续为这个社区应得的透明度而战。
