Let me tell you something absolutely BONKERS from last night’s midterms…

Democrat Ericka Lomick just “won” Texas House District 93 despite being a convicted felon who suspended her campaign months ago.

She pleaded guilty in 2011 to federal charges including mortgage-fraud conspiracy, bank fraud, and money laundering. Her sentence? 63 months in federal prison.

On her candidate paperwork, she checked the box claiming she had not been finally convicted of a felony. After her criminal record surfaced in September, she suspended her campaign and stopped running.

But Texas election deadlines had already passed, so her name remained on the ballot for both the regular general election and the special election.

And voters still elected her by roughly 51–49%.

Here’s the kicker: Under Texas law, a final felony conviction generally makes someone ineligible to hold office unless they’ve been pardoned or had their disabilities released.

Meaning she can’t actually serve. Her “victory” simply creates a vacancy and triggers yet another special election.

A convicted federal fraudster who quit campaigning still got elected to the Texas House.

Let that absolutely sink in.

text:
Every engineering org is thinking about how to harden their code right now. Formal verification, TLA+, simulation testing, more human review are all approaches being used rn.

These are great but very few people are talking about the underlying problem. Formal methods are good when the spec is precise and stable: protocols, kernels, compilers but not great at all for business applications. “A customer can’t check out with an empty cart” could be written in TLA+, but almost nobody will, because 1 business rules can change every week 2 keeping a formal model in sync with them is another layer of artifacts to keep in sync. And even then, you’ve verified the model, not the code thats running. 

The real problem with AI code gen is spec drift (and the bigger problem is actually intent drift but that's getting too meta). Before codegen, we had PMs, spec docs, tickets and code review to keep those aligned. That process can’t keep up with the speed we generate code now. Spec driven development is a step in the right direction, but it still generates code from the spec which run the same risk of drift aing part. Plus, the bigger issue is that there's nothing coupling your INTENT with the spec with the code.

We’re exploring a different idea: what if you throw the code out, and the spec IS what runs on the runtime?
I’m by no means a formal methods expert, but if you are, or you’re just as interested in the thesis that spec drift is the real problem hmu I’ll take you to lunch in SF this week so we can yap

text:
Google 在五国推出自愿离职补偿，最多给 12 个月工资

Google 正在出钱请部分员工主动离职。路透社 11 月 4 日独家报道，Google 从今年 6 月起，向加拿大、法国、德国、日本和瑞士的部分员工提供“自愿离职补偿”，负责 AI 研究的 DeepMind 部门不在其中。

这种做法和裁员不同。裁员是公司决定让谁走；自愿离职计划是公司先开出补偿条件，员工自己决定要不要申请，申请通过后拿一笔补偿金离开。

Google 向路透社确认了这件事。Google 发言人说，2025 年公司部分团队推出了带补偿金的自愿离职计划，今年 6 月又把它扩展到“几个国家”，目的是“支持接下来的重要工作”。这一轮之前没有被报道过，路透社没能查到有多少人接受。

【补偿给多少】

瑞士的情况最具体。Google 在瑞士有大约 5000 名员工，苏黎世是它的一个主要工程中心。据三名知情人士说，Google 在 6 月中旬公布方案，7 月中旬前答复了申请的员工，8 月开始有人离开。

接受的员工每工作一年拿一个月工资，最多 12 个月。也就是说，工作满 5 年拿 5 个月工资，工作满 15 年也只拿 12 个月。

其中一名知情人士说，在一个约 50 人的团队里，至少有 4 人接受了。瑞士这一轮覆盖多个部门，但不包括 DeepMind。

【哪些人不在名单里】

Google Cloud 和 DeepMind 的员工，过去几轮都没有被纳入。路透社说，这次扩展看起来也是同样的安排。Google 的母公司叫 Alphabet，它的首席财务官 Anat Ashkenazi 在季度财报会上多次说，AI 和云计算是招聘重点。

【计划的来历】

这个计划不是今年才有。去年起，Google 已经在美国和英国的部分部门推行过。公司高管把它说成是给“不再认同公司节奏或方向”的员工的一个选择。路透社说，至少有一个部门在自愿离职之后又进行了裁员。

路透社把这件事放在 AI 投入的背景下报道：Alphabet 在 AI 上花的钱越来越多，让华尔街投资者不安，也压低了它的股价，Google 想借此控制成本。Alphabet 的员工总数近几个季度在稳定增长，同时公司在把人力往重点领域调。上周，微软也向 6 万名员工提供了自愿离职补偿，目的同样是控制成本。

Google 在瑞士有过裁员先例：2023 年它在瑞士裁掉 200 多人，引发员工抗议和集体离岗。

And further supply tightening with Samsung/Micron discontinuing DDR2/DDR3 lines.

Winbond was leaving DDR2 lines to pursue higher end memory. People keep saying China, but even Gigadevice was leaving DDR3 to pursue higher end memory. "DDR3's share of our DRAM revenue will continue to decline until we eventually stop selling DDR3 products."Nanya discontinued DDR2 lines few days ago. 

This is while majority of ESMT revenue comes from DDR2/DDR3. In ~3 quarters of constant earnings, ESMT would have more assets than their entire MC.

Who is going to stop buying $40 DLink cameras if their $3 memory cost goes to $3.5?

$MU / Samsung / $SKHY / $SNDK share similar parallels where durability is contractually enforced via take/pay LTAs with price floors.

But markets are pretending that it just won't happen, despite Samsung already being the most profitable company in the world. 

Markets should care about how much FCF is actually hitting the balance sheets, but are just indiscriminately selling off everything now.

But continue rotating capital into 47x P/E companies like Walmart or 180x forward P/E names like $CRWD.

text:
为什么民主党横扫国会，先遭殃的却是AI股？

前几天，ABC新闻和《华盛顿邮报》做过一项民调，结果相当惊人。

72%的美国人反对在自己社区新建数据中心。

其中，民主党支持者的反对比例高达81%，共和党支持者也有58%。

大家都希望AI越来越聪明，最好什么活都能替自己干。但是，你要在我家附近建一个巨型机房？

不好意思，免谈。

这背后其实有个很现实的问题。

AI赚的钱，老百姓没分到多少，但AI消耗的电，大家却可能要一起买单。

你想想，微软、谷歌、亚马逊每年拿出几千亿美元，疯狂采购GPU、建设数据中心。

这些东西不是凭空运转的。它们需要大量电力、冷却用水，还需要扩建变电站和输电网络。

问题来了，这些基础设施的钱谁出？

MIT今年的一项研究发现，数据中心进入当地市场后，居民电价平均上涨约2.1%。

这个数字看起来不大，但对本来就被通胀折腾得够呛的美国家庭来说，已经足够让人不满了。

更让人心理不平衡的是，科技巨头有时候还能拿到政府的税收优惠。

你是全球最有钱的公司之一，跑来我们这里建机房，占用土地和水电资源，政府还给你减税？

这笔账，老百姓越算越不对劲。

于是，一个非常有意思的政治现象出现了。

反对AI数据中心，居然开始成为美国政客争取选票的武器。

最典型的就是得克萨斯州。

大家知道，得州原本是美国AI基建最火热的地方之一。土地多、能源丰富，科技巨头都想去那里建数据中心。

结果这次选举，民主党候选人Gina Hinojosa居然击败了长期执政的共和党州长Abbott。

而她的竞选主张之一，就是暂停新的数据中心开发审批，收紧水电使用监管，取消相关税收优惠。

这还不是民主党单方面的事情。

连共和党籍的Abbott此前都已经宣布暂停部分数据中心审批，因为当地居民的反对声音实在太大。

你看，政治人物可能在很多问题上吵得不可开交，但一旦涉及老百姓的钱包，立场就开始趋同了。

更夸张的是，今年美国有10个州，把涉及数据中心的41项地方议案摆上了选票。

以前地方政府为了吸引科技巨头，恨不得送地、减税、帮忙修电网。

现在风向反过来了。

你想来建机房？可以，先问问当地居民答不答应。

以前市场想得特别简单。

微软明年还要增加资本开支，谷歌还要买更多GPU，亚马逊还要建更多机房。

所以英伟达订单继续增长，存储芯片继续涨价，服务器、电力设备一路受益。

大家都按照未来几年AI基础设施疯狂扩张的速度，给整条产业链定价。

但现在突然多了一个问题。

钱有了，芯片也订了，结果地方政府不让你建，或者要求你自己承担更多电网、供水成本。

怎么办？

项目可能得延期，投资回报周期被拉长，原本预计明年兑现的收入，可能要后年才能兑现。

对于微软、谷歌这种现金充足的巨头，或许还能承受。

但对那些借了大量资金建设数据中心的公司来说，可就难受了。

投资人已经开始担心，有些AI公司还没等到赚大钱的那一天，先被沉重的融资成本压得喘不过气了。

如果未来地方政府再限制数据中心建设，项目一延期，利息还得继续付。

这就是华尔街最害怕的事情：

AI需求明明还在增长，但其中一部分公司的现金流，可能已经撑不起市场之前预想的扩张速度。

当然，也不能说民主党赢了，AI革命就要完蛋。

毕竟懂王还有否决权，民主党也没法随便通过一项法律，就把美国的数据中心全部叫停。

有些项目大概率只是从一个州搬到另一个州，需求未必真的消失。

甚至对于已经拥有电网接入许可、稳定电力资源的数据中心来说，新项目审批越难，现有资源反而可能越值钱。

所以，AI革命的成本，到底应该由谁来承担？

You guys lost because of the war, and turned on every single promise you made in 2024

author: aaalex
quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

text: orgo is the defacto standard for giving your agent a computer
author: nickvasilescu
quoted_text:
running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian

my team is 50+ people in 12 countries, but i talk to my agents more than my human teammates

- voice note to grokbot
- mattpocock/skills /grill-me so the agent interrogates the idea before anything gets built
- spec drops into linear through the linear mcp
- exa + firecrawl agent reads every competitor site, pricing page and changelog
- https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA to find ideas and trends
- apify pulls g2, reddit and app store reviews
- prompt: "find the 10 complaints that show up most and quote the users"
- context7 so the agent reads the latest docs before it touches any api

the design

- claude code + paper mcp
- 4 versions of every screen before a single line of code
- pick pieces from 2, it merges them. diverge then converge
- frontend-design skill from anthropic/skills + our own design system skill
- cleanshot screenshots of any ui i like go straight in with "make it feel like this"

the build

- pingdotgg/t3code as the control surface for every agent, from my phone too
- stablyai/orca runs a fleet of agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree
- graphify maps the whole codebase into a knowledge graph so agents navigate instead of guess
- headroom compresses tool outputs before they hit the model, so tokens go 20-95% further
- lsp plugins so the agent sees types and errors like an ide does
- security guidance hook flags risky edits before they land
- supabase mcp for the database, stripe for billing
- github mcp opens the pr, vercel spins up a preview
- loops run overnight, i check what shipped over coffee

the user testing

- lightpanda as the headless browser, way lighter than chromium so you can run hundreds at once
- agents click every flow on the preview like a first-time user
- one persona is impatient, one is confused, one is on a phone
- playwright + chrome devtools mcp for regression tests

the bugs

- sentry mcp catches the error
- agent reads the stack trace and opens a fix pr in under 10 minutes
- human just approves

the data

- posthog mcp cron at 7am on yesterday's funnel
- any step that drops more than 10%, the agent watches 20 session replays and tells me why
- stripe mcp pulls every cancellation reason into one doc every monday

the agents' tools

- orgo so every agent gets its own computer
- agentmail so every agent gets its own inbox
- agentphone so i can call them from the car
- composio connect-apps for every other connector
- akitaonrails/ai-memory, a git-backed markdown wiki so they remember what we decided last week

the skills

- wshobson/agents so skills work across claude code, codex and opencode
- my writing voice
- our design system
- how we write specs
- skill creator so the agents write new skills themselves

some helpful tricks

- one agent per platform. the x agent never touches email
- cheap model for triage, opus for anything that ships

We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

quoted_text:
Is Morpho trying to kill DeFi? 

@aave and @Morpho both sent the SEC a legal framework for DeFi lending, one defends DeFi, the other negotiates it away

When you deposit into a lending market or a vault, did you just buy a security? If yes, someone has to register, disclose and answer to the SEC. If no, DeFi keeps running as it is.

The SEC mainly uses two tests: 

1- Howey: did you put money into a shared venture and expect profit from someone else's work? 

2- Reves: is your position really an IOU, a note someone promised to repay?  

Aave's approach (Aave Labs, @kamino , @veda_labs ) On Howey, there is no shared venture. Suppliers use the same pool and rate, but nobody's profit depends on anyone else. DAO votes with timelocks run a market. They don't manage your money

On Reves, the test never starts, as there is no lender, no borrower duty and no promise to repay, so no IOU exists. Vault curators may count as investment advisers, yet they can't touch your funds

That means no custody and no fund. What it wants from the SEC: confirm existing law. No exemption needed

Morpho's approach (CCI Vault Coalition: Morpho, Bitwise, Galaxy) Control is the yardstick. The less any person can change after you deposit, the further you sit from securities law. Ten conditions define the safe zone, including locked or timelocked parameters and no moving funds between markets after deposit

Howey gets fought mostly on "someone else's work." The paper concedes a vault may already count as a shared venture

Lending positions are treated as notes under Reves, and selling them to retail likely leans "security," it admits.

Its request: exemptive relief, a compliance entity wherever someone holds control, and a private fund lane for vetted investors.

So what's best for DeFi?

Morpho's map is detailed and candid about hard cases, which regulators appreciate. The cost is ground given up before the fight begins. Every concession becomes the SEC's starting point, and the safe zone rewards frozen code over protocols that keep evolving. Aave keeps the default where DeFi needs it. Open markets aren't securities, governance can keep improving the protocol, and no company has to stand in front of it.

Adopt Aave's reading and DeFi stays permissionless, but under Morpho's, DeFi runs on a license

BREAKING: Banks and regulators in 6 countries are now on alert for AI and cyber fraud.

This is what Covid looked like in week 1. A few countries. Small numbers. Nobody called it a crisis.

1/ Switzerland: since November 1, the regulator FINMA demands tougher online ID checks to stop deepfakes and fake identities. Liveness checks, proof that a real person and not a photo or a deepfake is on camera, now cover more ID routes.

2/ Canada: Royal Bank of Canada now blocks outside AI agents from online banking. The regulator recommends human approval for high-impact actions an AI takes.

3/ USA: in one week, JPMorgan, Citi and Schwab blocked outside AI agents from customer accounts. Schwab says unauthorized agents try to move client money 10 to 20 times a week. Wells Fargo's answer: from November 24, AI agent use is "at your own risk".

4/ South Korea: since late September, at least 9 banks were targeted by hacks. CrowdStrike says the attacker likely used an AI agent. At Shinhan Bank alone, personal data of about 25,000 customers was exposed.

5/ Italy, earlier this year: one fake WhatsApp from "the CEO", one AI-cloned voice. Intesa Sanpaolo's private bank sent €95 million (about $108 million). About €36 million is still gone, turned into crypto.

6/ France: a FIRST for a French bank. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa confirmed an attack. More than $133 million (€118 million) was pulled out over several days, French press says, and $63 million of it was swapped into Ether in just 4 hours. This morning, customers couldn't even log in to the app.

Now zoom out.

AI can now fake a voice, a face and an ID. Accounts opened with fake IDs passed the checks. The money moves in hours. On the blockchain, an investigator traced the French money before the bank even confirmed the attack. For customers, the visible sign was an app that wouldn't let them in.

Covid locked the streets. This one can lock your money. Nobody is calling this a crisis yet. But the regulators already plan for the day it hits every bank.

23 European countries told their people to stock up on food. The rules that protect the money in your bank app are only being written now.

The ECB gave eurozone banks until October 31 to hand in their AI cyber defence plans. And today, one more government sent lenders and fintech firms an advisory on AI-assisted cyber fraud. It recommends payment limits, receiver checks and switching off payment channels nobody uses.

This is week 1. Be prepared.

The next $133 million could leave a bank you use. Follow me now, so you don't first hear about it from an app that won't open.

A few observations on this market and what I think people need to understand if they genuinely want to become better traders.

First, I keep seeing this divide between people who believe in building long-term community coins and those who trade the daily attention-driven runners. I genuinely don't understand why we pretend one approach has to invalidate the other.

I trade both. That's simply how this market operates.

Every single day, there's a new coin capturing attention, attracting liquidity and giving traders a window of opportunity to make money. Some of these plays last a few hours, others a few days, and occasionally one develops into something much bigger.
There's absolutely nothing wrong with participating in that.

I think a lot of the frustration towards these daily runners comes from people sitting in community coins that aren't getting the attention or bids they believe they deserve. I understand that frustration, but getting upset at other people for trading what's moving isn't going to bring liquidity into your bags.
Attention is what drives this market. Conviction is what can sustain it. Both have their place.

Secondly, let's talk about callouts and KOLs.

I've always encouraged people to do their own research before blindly buying something because someone with a following posted it. Following good traders can absolutely help you discover opportunities earlier, but you need to understand that not everyone in this space has the same intentions.
Some genuinely want to find good opportunities and share them with their communities. Others might be more interested in using their audience as exit liquidity. Learning to distinguish between the two is part of becoming a better trader.

I get accused of farming rewards almost daily. At this point, I've accepted that people will believe whatever they want. I know how I trade, what my intentions are and how much effort I put into finding opportunities. I don't feel the need to prove that to strangers every day.
What Pumpfun has built is an ecosystem that accommodates all kinds of traders. Short-term momentum traders, long-term conviction holders, community builders, callers and everyone in between.

That's a good thing. We shouldn't be trying to turn everyone into the same type of trader.

The goal isn't to convince everyone to trade like you. It's to understand how the market works well enough to find your own edge.

Learn when to follow attention, when to exercise patience, when to take profits and, most importantly, when you're wrong.

You don't have to marry every coin, and you don't have to sell every coin after 20 minutes.

There's room for both approaches. The sooner people understand that, the better traders they'll become.

text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8
author: AnthropicAI

text: Vaults are the largest ribonucleoprotein particles in eukaryotic cells, built from 78 copies of the major vault protein (MVP), yet their function remains unknown four decades after their discovery. MVP homologs occur in prokaryotes and bacteriophages, but whether they form vaults is unknown. Here, we show that prokaryotic and bacteriophage MVP homologs assemble into vault particles. We surveyed approximately 15 billion proteins, found MVP homologs in 29 bacterial and 4 archaeal phyla, and used size-exclusion chromatography to rapidly screen and isolate vault particles of eight homologs expressed in Escherichia coli. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of the phage homolog L05 at high resolution reveal a shell of 96 MVP chains enclosing a volume ~25% larger than human vaults, among the largest protein shells of defined size outside virus capsids. Prokaryotic MVPs typically carry seven wall repeats and eukaryotic MVPs nine, and adding wall repeats to L05 yields larger vaults. Prokaryotic vaults expand the known diversity of vault architecture and offer a tractable system for studying vault assembly and a size-tunable scaffold for cargo encapsulation.

Head of Engineering at Sovright, Zaki Manian reveals how an Anthropic AI model uncovered a major Zcash vulnerability that could have allowed anyone to create money out of thin air:

"People had been doing AI-driven audits. Tailor had been running one and basically the day Opus 4.8 came out, which was in May, Tailor had been running a standard set of queries across the Zcash codebase."   

"Opus 4.8 comes out from Anthropic and finds the worst... what is called in the parlance of zero-knowledge proofs a soundness vulnerability." 

"A soundness vulnerability is a very benign sounding term for basically the worst possible vulnerability you could have in a zero-knowledge proof protocol, which is you can forge a proof and therefore you can create money from nothing."   

"So it got patched fairly quietly and then after it was patched Zuko wrote a Twitter X article that was basically: 'This is what this vulnerability meant and how bad it could have been.'"

text:
🖤Burned Soul: Ash and Ice🖤

For too long and too stubbornly they tried to remake her.

Not simply to correct — but to cut away the excess, smooth the edges, make her convenient. Manipulations settled in a thin film, control tightened around her ribs, cruelty burned out whatever still breathed. They approached her as raw material: “there’s too much here,” “be quieter,” “don’t feel so deeply,” “be like this.” They tried to break her and put her back together — for themselves, for their fears, for their ideas of what a woman should be if she is to be endured.

She bent, but she did not break. And at first she burned. 

She flared like a typhoon — with a wild, uncontrollable passion that swept away everything in its path. Then, suddenly, she would become tender to the point of pain, and that tenderness cut deeper than any hardness. A mixture no one knew how to hold.

Some feared her strength and tried to mute it. Others feared the tenderness and began to wound her so she would become “normal” again.

In the end, everything inside burned out completely. Not even coal remained — only gray, silent ash. And over it lay ice. Thin, transparent, almost invisible. 
Words pass through her: she looks at people, hears the words, answers in the right places — and feels nothing. Neither hurt, nor anger, nor warmth. Only a cold, even mask behind which nothing living remains.

And yet somewhere deep, beneath the layer of ice and ash, a tiny flame still burns. It does not warm, but it remembers who she truly is.

Passionate to the point of trembling. A little mad, tender to the point of pain, capable of driving someone mad with a single glance and giving herself entirely — without remainder and without conditions.

It simply hopes that one day someone will appear who sees this strength and is not afraid. Who will not try to remake her. Who will simply accept her as she is.

🖤🩷And then the ice will crack — not from pressure, but because this burned soul will flare once more into a bright flame.🔥

text:
我们 SGLang Omni 团队在中东的独苗，@ratishp22 要去 MBZUAI 的 IFM 担任 Research Scientist  了，和我的好朋友佘建树大哥一起工作。

他高兴的与我分享 offer letter 那天，我由衷为他自豪，也有些舍不得。

今年年初，这次是第一次在 Slack 上找我，那个时候 AI coding 已经泛滥成灾了。于我看来，我担心他也是一个用 AI Slop 攻击 SGLang 仓库的随机开发者。因此我并未如何理会他，直到我发现他的坚持且对我的 comments 改动都非常细心，这是一个非常好的开始。

于是，从今年一月开始，刚开始和我一起做 SGLang 的时候，他就一直是一个非常负责且积极的状态。交给他的事，他都能条理清晰记清楚，快速实现且反馈，也做得很认真。但那时候他不太自信，状态也不算好，总担心自己做得不够好（其实他现在也不太自信 😂，但是这不掩盖他的优秀）。

这种感觉我能理解。刚进一个陌生的大项目，大多数人都和他不在一个时区，自然会有所犹豫。

这一年，我们从 Miles 一路攻坚克难到 SGLang-Omni，我看着他在开源社区的巨大进步。

每次 SGLang 版本升级，Omni 都要跟着适配对应的 API 接口。这件事自然是脏活累活，做好了也没什么人注意，吃力不讨好。Ratish 前后做了七次，将遇到的坑写成了文档，尤其是那些不报错的静默错误。SGLang-Omni 现在可以直接 pip install。第一个 PyPI 包是我和 huapeng 发的，但是从 0.1.0 之后，每一个版本的发版，都是 Ratish 全权负责。

此外，我们的多硬件生态也由他主力完成：一份 RFC 将事情拆清楚，然后 Intel、AMD、华为、摩尔线程的工程师陆续来提 PR，他一个一个 review，与合作的硬件厂朋友们不厌其烦进行反复的测试和验证。现在，SGLang-Omni 能跑在丰富的硬件平台上，我们也希望继续深入推动，甚至是本地的 MLX 生态。

过去的半年，他几乎每天都有 PR 合入，数量已经无法证明他的优秀程度了。他做事踏实、勤恳，交上来的东西都有数据、有验证。当然，权责对等，出了问题，我知道他会负责到底。

现在的他，理解如何自己写 RFC、定方向，会 review 乃至 fight back 别人的代码。我想，自信大概就是这样一点点攒出来的。

过去一段时间，我们也帮他推荐了一些机会。他面了新加坡、美国，还有阿联酋本地的几家 startup/大厂，最后选择去 MBZUAI 的 IFM，和我的好大哥佘建树一起工作。我相信他在那里会有很好的发展，也期待他永远留在开源社区。

还有一件事，我一直想说。我英语不好，本身也不太擅长和英文母语的人沟通。和 Ratish 的交流，对我帮助很大。他也经常要把我的话放进翻译软件，才能弄明白我想说什么。想到这里，我一直很不好意思，确实给他添了很多麻烦。（PS：微信自带的翻译具有最好的上下文，但是翻译效果其实并不太完美 😂）

SGLang-Omni 最开始只有三个人：我、Ratish 和景文。现在，项目里有超过 20 位 active maintainer，everything in law and order。

我们永远欢迎更多人加入，我们也永远会推荐最好的机会给大家。唯一的核心便是权责对等：为这个项目扛起多少责任，就会得到相应的权利和 credit。

也欢迎大家多多帮我们宣传宣传。SGLang-Omni 是一个严肃的项目，是有人负责的。我们也用 AI 写代码，但这不是一个用 AI 随便写出的玩具，这是严肃的 interactive model 所依赖的生产力工具。每一块代码背后都能找到负责的人，出了问题，永远有人站出来解决，Ratish 也是其中一员。

最后，恭喜 Ratish，恭喜你！祝你在 IFM 一切顺利，期待我们能够在不远的将来见到彼此，也欢迎你到美国或者中国、新加坡的时候，和社区的伙伴们热烈相聚！

text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

text:
Scale AI 创始人 Alexandr Wang 最近在 YC 的一场对谈，讲了一个非常重要的判断：未来最稀缺的资源，不是智力，不是执行力，而是野心。

19岁创办 Scale AI，如今执掌 Meta 超级智能实验室，Alexandr Wang 对 AI 时代的创业机会有几个非常值得思考的观点。

1. 即使 AI 从今天开始停止进步，人类仍有几十年的红利。

现有 AI 能力远远没有被充分使用。仅仅把今天的技术推广到所有行业，就足以带来几十年的经济变革。

2. AI 时代，真正稀缺的是愿景。

过去创业需要大量人才、资本和技术积累。未来智能和执行力可能越来越便宜，真正稀缺的是你能否想象5～10年后的世界，以及有没有野心把它变成现实。

3. 创业公司第一次有机会成为“机甲巨人”。

传统大公司是巨人，但拥抱 AI Agent 的创业公司，相当于给自己穿上了机甲。小团队可能拥有过去几百人才能实现的执行能力。

4. 伟大的机会往往始于非共识。

当年创办 Scale AI，投资人普遍不看好数据标注，认为这不是长期生意。

但 Wang 从第一性原理出发：训练 AI 需要算力、代码和数据，前两者容易获取，唯独数据是瓶颈。

如今，数据已经成为 AI 产业最重要的战略资源之一。

5. 押注世界上最陡峭、持续时间最长的指数曲线。

过去是摩尔定律，现在是 AI。

重要的不是今天的产品看起来有多酷，而是你所做的事情，是否站在一条持续十年以上的增长曲线上。

未来最贵的，可能不是 Intelligence，而是 Ambition。

text:
🧐 What does a surge in immigration do to an economy? I went looking for answers in the official numbers instead of the shouting. Some of what I found surprised me.

📊 Start with scale. U.S. Customs and Border Protection recorded 2,475,669 encounters at the southwest border in FY2023, the highest on record, and 2,135,005 in FY2024. [1] That's more encounters than Houston has residents (2.4 million, Census 2025 estimate), though an encounter is an event, not a person, and one person can be counted more than once. [10]

💵 Question 1: Does it grow the economy? On paper, yes. The Congressional Budget Office projects the 2021–2026 immigration surge adds $8.9 trillion to nominal GDP over 2024–2034 and lowers federal deficits by $0.9 trillion, mostly through income and payroll taxes. CBO itself calls the estimates "very uncertain." [2]

🏛️ Question 2: Who pays up front? Here's the twist. The gains show up in federal ledgers, but CBO estimates the same surge cost state and local governments a net $9.2 billion in 2023. More than half of the spending went to K-12 education, shelter and border security. [3]

👨‍👩‍👧 Question 3: Is it a cost or an investment? The answer depends on which generation you look at. The National Academies found first-generation immigrants cost governments more than the native-born, while their children are "among the strongest fiscal and economic contributors in the U.S." [4] The ledger is a 30-year story, not a one-year snapshot.

🏫 Schools: Since Plyler v. Doe (1982), states can't deny children a free public education based on immigration status. [5] That's a fixed cost with a long payoff.

🚑 Emergency rooms: Under the federal EMTALA law, hospitals that take Medicare and run an ER must screen and stabilize anyone with an emergency "regardless of ability to pay." [6] The ER is the one door in American health care that is legally always open.

🩺 Doctors: The Association of American Medical Colleges projects a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, driven mainly by population growth and aging. [7] More people means more patients, and also more potential health workers, so the shortage cuts both ways.

🚓 Law enforcement: This is where intuition and data part ways. A peer-reviewed Texas study in PNAS (2020) found undocumented immigrants had substantially lower felony arrest rates than native-born citizens. [8] Even so, CBO counts state border-security spending (law enforcement against illegal crossings, smuggling and trafficking, plus barriers and transporting immigrants between states) as part of that $9.2 billion. [3]

🌍 Question 4: What happens when coverage is universal? England's NHS is a useful test case. In August 2026, 7.4 million cases were waiting for treatment, and only 65.2% had waited under 18 weeks, against a 92% standard. [9] In Canada, 68% of hip and 61% of knee replacements were done within the 6-month benchmark in 2024 (CIHI). [11] Covering everyone is one problem. Having enough doctors to see them is another.

🤔 My take: Both sides of the ledger are real. Immigration looks like a long-run economic gain and a short-run local bill, and the hospitals, classrooms and city budgets that pay first aren't the ones that collect the payroll taxes. Any serious debate has to be about timing and capacity, not just headcount. That mismatch is the most interesting fact in this whole story.

🔗 Sources:
[1] CBP, Southwest Land Border Encounters: https://t.co/JLsUYusGgC (FY totals also in CRS IN12457: https://t.co/z9UgKJavlo)
[2] CBO, July 2024: https://t.co/qnNLMAzm8A
[3] CBO, June 2025: https://t.co/KX9LtDFyhJ
[4] National Academies, 2016: https://t.co/WbqcQUia9V
[5] Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202: https://t.co/MkoyeJ3KIc
[6] CMS, EMTALA: https://t.co/WFgKi1yIjb
[7] AAMC, Mar. 2024: https://t.co/vslh7CcGlK
[8] Light et al., PNAS 2020: https://t.co/iIL74u2FU9
[9] NHS England RTT, Aug. 2026: https://t.co/6Qx1Ddv3fT
[10] U.S. Census Bureau, QuickFacts, Houston city, Texas: https://t.co/wavNfTIEtQ
[11] CIHI, Wait Times for Priority Procedures in Canada, 2025: https://t.co/RLvi8XPlpp

quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

text:
The human body as the moat. 

I recently applied to Config to speak about Chipped as part of my Do Hard Things/Rejection Therapy challenge. Talking about Chipped is often hard for me, because all I see are the failures that came with it. But one thing I do find fascinating, and really want to talk about, is the human body as the sandbox, the human body as the operating system, and the failures that come with that when you build a technical product you can't control in its entirety. What does that three percent of failure rate do to a product?

I think about the human body a lot, not just how the body and technology fail together, but the limitations of the body itself. That's why I love endurance and distance sports so much, and I always have. Now, more than ever, the human being is the moat. I joke that the last remaining job is a personality hire, but at the end of the day, I think it's true.

Reflecting on what I loved so much about growing Chipped, it was the difficult parts. Building the app, the product, the supply chain, all the moving parts was hard, but so much fun, and I loved it. Now I feel like I'm one-shotting ideas within two hours, and the joy of the grind is gone. I think that's why I've gone so deep into my endurance training, and why I'm about to pay a deposit on something mammoth for next year. Because it's like, okay, I can do so much with AI, but what can I do with myself? You can't cheat it. You can't fake it. You can't vibe code. You can't fake a time. 

What your body can physically achieve as a human being can be amplified by AI, but I do not deny there is the bubble we live in here that is of very little interest to the outside world. I think the most impressive thing from here on will be the human being.

Last night was special.

Election days just never get old for us at Polymarket. Watching regular people experience the beauty of market based forecasts as the results come in. How practically useful it is. How simple it is to interpret. When it clicks, it clicks.

It’s now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks. The networks hold out until absolute certainty, and the suspense keeps it entertaining all night. No knock to them, but now there’s Polymarket, and many people are realizing they want to know what's happening in real time.

I know the industry has gained a mixed rap for a variety of reasons, many of which are criticisms with real merit. But I think I speak for both myself and my peers when I say we got into this because we really love the idea of markets being able to place a price on the future (e.g. Democrats had a 92% chance to take the House on Polymarket), and how that can help people better understand what's likely to happen and make decisions accordingly.

Our mission is to make sure we deliver on the promise of prediction markets, which was on full display last night. In the midst of so much noise around what we do, the American people get to see what Polymarket is really all about. Feels like one step closer to the dream. Onwards.

text: Check out Joules to GDP, which makes it possible for us to measure the economic value per unit of energy spent on compute!
author: KyeGomezB
quoted_text:
AI is using more and more of the world’s energy. But how much economic value are we getting from AI?

We’re introducing Joules-to-GDP (J2G), a framework that measures how well AI turns energy into economic value and shows which tasks, models, and hardware give the best return.

Across 44 occupations in finance, engineering, law, administrative work, and more in @OpenAI's GDPval, we arrive at three findings:

1) The tasks with the highest economic value are not the tasks with the highest economic value per joule. For example, CAD design earns ~10% more per task than building websites, but the latter earns ~27% more value per joule.

2) The most powerful model isn’t always the best use of energy. Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of GLM 5.2’s net value with 23% of the energy, for 2.5x the value per joule.

3) More chips don’t guarantee proportionate returns. Moving the same model from 1 to 8 NVIDIA H100s uses 3.2x the energy but cuts completion time by only 22%, with about the same value.

With @SnorkelAI, we’re also releasing GDPWorks, a benchmark for economically valuable tasks across 36 additional occupations.

Joint work co-led by @amirzeinaalii and @Avanika15, with @Mersad_Abbasi, @Jon_Hartley_, John Hennessy, @HazyResearch, and @Azaliamirh.

More details below 🧵

quoted_text:
Clanker: Reboot.

2 years ago (almost to the day), Clanker was born over on the original Farcaster app. The idea was simple: Make it possible for anyone to launch a token just by posting on the timeline and tagging @clanker_world. 

The timing was right, and it caught on like wildfire. Suddenly, even people who never thought they’d launch a token were trying it out in the feed. (I even clanked my first meme token on day 1 to see how it all worked. If you search hard, you can probably find it.)

Over the ensuing year, Clanker went on a genny run, expanding from Fc to the X feed and becoming the highest volume launchpad on @base by far, birthing some of the most iconic tokens & token communities of that era, including BNKR, DRB, FAIR & more. 

So many builders on Farcaster & beyond turned to Clanker to bootstrap their ideas & find their first 1,000 true fans. Legends like @0FJAKE, @AtownBrown, @david_tomu and @darkohh clanked tokens for their projects. Some, like @MLeeJr, even took it upon themselves to clank tokens for OTHER people’s projects.

And when @netnose and I decided to build a gacha app for creator discovery, we clanked our native token on day one too.

There’s just always been something fundamentally OP about clanking tokens right in the feed. Social graph integration remains undefeated in the attention economy. 

But despite all this pedigree & lore, Clanker has had… a rough time lately, to say the least. Between early founder drama, the sale to Farcaster and the eventual handoff to Neynar, Clanker’s been like a teenager who hasn’t been allowed to finish a full year at the same school. How can you even make friends like that?

Hopefully, that all changes today.

Clanker is in good hands now with @masknetwork (stewards of Firefly and Lens Protocol), and they’ve partnered with one of the best engineering teams in the space to give Clanker a much-needed Reboot. More on that soon, but in the meantime…

I’m excited to announce that I’ve accepted the role of Clanker CEO and will be taking on the challenge of guiding our beloved tokenbot back to its former glory.

Transparently, this wasn’t a decision I took lightly. I’ve been self-employed since I was 17, and always preferred to work on things I founded myself. But Clanker has held a very special place in my heart since day 1, and I feel like the little guy’s been a victim of circumstance for much of the past 18 months. He deserves a second chance at romance, and I’m honored to be the one to lead the charge. 

I’m also grateful to everyone who helped make Clanker what it is today. To Proxy and Jack for the founder energy, to Base and Farcaster for backing the ecosystem, to communities like DRB and Bankr for keeping it alive, and to @ProfWerder & @age_shulman for their stewardship too. The fact that this little tokenbot has survived all these seasons is crazy in its own right. We stand on the shoulders of giants.

Much more to come from me soon, but here are my main priorities to start:

- Reboot and refresh the Clanker brand without losing its special je ne sais quoi.

- Work with our socials guru @stanisloou to keep comms fresh and clean.

- Work with our engineering team to bring clanker features up to parity with modern launchpads (stock pairs, new chains and even day one support for _______)

- Rebuild the trust that has been lost with both builders & trenchers through all these transitions.

- Show up for OG communities who are still here building and shipping two years later.

- Bring new launch energy back to Clanker & back to the feed, where distribution is built-in by default. 

So if you’re looking to launch a funny meme, a clever stock pair, or an app coin to bootstrap your project, I want to help you succeed. 

Same goes if you’re a builder with an idea to build on top of clanker protocol; the energy here has always been collaborative and that won’t change. 

My DMs are open and we can win together. 

Let’s press REBOOT and run it back turbo. 

Clank Clank!

text:
Traditional sparse attention only attends to a subset of tokens, but its indexer still scores every single key to find them. At 100k+ context, searching for the needles takes longer than actually computing attention.

The LSA intuition: instead of scoring every key or chunking by position, LSA groups keys into semantic clusters in latent space. Queries score the clusters first, then only evaluate keys inside the winning clusters—turning an O(N²) brute-force scan into a subquadratic hierarchical lookup.
author: Raullen
quoted_text:
We got Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) running end-to-end on Apple Silicon—and found a hybrid approach that gets the best of both worlds 👀
Qwen3.8-27B on M3 Ultra (128k context):
• Time to first token: 640s → 440s (−31%) 
• Peak memory: 40.7 GB → 28.8 GB (−29%) 
• MTP decode speed: Zero regression

The insight: Use LSA only to digest the prompt, then hand off to standard MTP for generation.

On Apple Silicon, pure LSA matches the paper's prefill scaling (1.16× faster at 64k, 1.41× at 128k), but slows down generation because per-token routing overhead hurts when decode is memory-bandwidth bound.

The fix: Sparse attention for compute-bound prefill, dense MTP for bandwidth-bound decode.

Next up: Qwen3.8-27B + GLM-5.3-Flash benchmarks across the M-series lineup. Stay tuned.

text:
These action scenes have nothing to do with each other. Could Firefly turn them into ONE cinematic showreel? 💥
That was the test: take my footage from different genres and bring it together into 60–90 seconds of action.

I wanted an opening that grabs you immediately, sharp cuts, a few moments to breathe, and a finale that hits hard.

I uploaded my clips into Adobe Firefly’s video editor and gave Quick Cut a prompt describing the direction I wanted. Then I moved into the timeline to refine the sequence and pacing.

That’s the part that interests me as a VFX artist: getting a first assembly to react to, then making the creative decisions that shape the final edit.

Which shot deserves to open the reel? Where should a moment last longer? Where does a cut make the action feel stronger?

Having the first cut and the timeline in the same workspace gives me a starting point I can keep working on.

Watch the showreel below. I’m also sharing the process with the full Firefly interface, from importing the footage to prompting Quick Cut and refining the edit, so you can follow the steps with your own clips. 👇

以下各项「均尚不属于普通股，因此不计入其中」：
· 尚未行权的期权

text:
有朋友问，为什么Texas这次这么多职位都翻蓝了？

选前几天，Ted Cruz在自己的播客里警告，共和党可能输掉得州每一个全州选举，结果真的发生了。我们先看一下规模。按得州州务卿网站11月4日下午的非正式计票，联邦参议员Talarico对Paxton，55%对43%；州长Hinojosa对现任Abbott，52.8%对45.7%；副州长、总检察长、财政审计长、土地专员、农业专员，民主党全都拿下，得票都在51%到53%之间。路透社说，这是1994年以来，民主党第一次在得州赢下全州选举。共和党在得州连着掌权三十年，一个晚上，从州长到农业专员，整班人换掉了。

那为什么是一整班，不像其他红州那样只翻一两个席位呢？因为这些职位虽然分开计票，投票的却是同一批人，在同一张选票上，对同一个执政团队下判断。一个选民要是觉得，问题不在哪一个官员，而在这一整套人怎么治理，他就会一路往下都换。看数字也是这样，除了Talarico多赢了一截，有他自己的原因，也有对手Paxton的包袱，其余几个职位的差距其实几乎一样，都在四到七个点之间，这更像是对整个执政团队的一次打分，不是每个民主党候选人都突然有了魅力。写政府论的时候我说，选票是一种打断，它的力气有限，不是每一次都换得动。这一次在得州，它一口气换掉了一整班人。

那选民在打分时，想的是什么？美联社的选民调查里，约两成得州选民说，通胀让家里“严重困难”，这些人里约四分之三投了Talarico；另有约六成说是“中等困难”，多数也投了他。两党的策略人士都说，关税和伊朗战争带来的经济压力，是最大的因素，文化议题这一次压不住生活成本。共和党顾问Garrett Fulce说得更直接，这是对党在全国和州一级的治理方式的“彻底否定”。

全国的不满，又落到了具体的地方。其中非常重要的一个就是学校。Abbott为了推动约十亿美元的教育储蓄账户，也就是用公款补贴私校的计划，2024年在初选里支持挑战者，把反对这项计划的本党州议员换掉。可在很多农村小镇，公立学校就是地方经济的一部分，学者选前就提醒，这会留下怨气，让一部分农村共和党人懒得出门投票。如果一个政府让人觉得，公立学校在它心里排到了私校补贴后面，那它还能不能持续得到民心，就要打个问号了。

另一个是数据中心。几个农村县起诉，要挡住数据中心建设，理由是用水、污染和农地；ABC、《华盛顿邮报》和益普索的民调说，69%的得州人反对在自己社区新建数据中心。一位一辈子投共和党的退伍海军陆战队员说，他家农场旁边要建一座，他打算这辈子第一次投民主党。写太空散热那篇我说，地上建数据中心，周围的居民至少还能去听证会上说话，在得州，他们用的是选票。

还有边境和郊区。2024年第一次翻红的Starr县，这一次大比例回到了民主党，共和党顾问估计，拉美裔选民的摆动有几十个点，移民执法很可能是关键。达拉斯郊区的Collin、Tarrant、Denton，2024年还投共和党，这次全州选举都站到了民主党一边。

当然候选人也有分别。共和党领导层原本觉得Cornyn更适合大选，Trump却力挺Paxton，Paxton在初选决选里赢了。美联社的调查里，约三分之二投参议员一票的人认为，Paxton缺乏当参议员的品格。共和党为保这个席位，花了超过三亿一千六百万美元。写Talarico那篇我说，钱买不到投票站那一下，这一次是真的买不到。

去年重划国会选区，Trump要得州多给共和党5个席位，结果在5个新划的选区里，共和党只保住1个，又丢了2个原有席位，最后反倒净输1席。民主党顾问Jim Wick说，重划靠的是一个假设，2024年为了经济投共和党的拉美裔选民，会一直留下来。选区可以画，人心靠画留不住。

不过，得州也不见得会就此永久变蓝。州参议院还在共和党手里，州众议院归谁还没定，新副州长的权力，也可能被州参议院改规则削掉一块。选民这次换掉的，是一个执政团队，不等于把全部主张都授权给了另一个。Talarico说过，得州最好的颜色是紫色，这样两党各级的政客都不敢懈怠，都得认真听选民的声音。我认同，而且这不仅仅是对德州的。

Hinojosa在选前说过一句话，民主党不是要结束一个一党独大的时代，再开启另一个。这句话要算数，就得让下一次的选票，也照样能把她们换掉。受问是常态，对谁都是。

text:
和历史上大多数有破坏性的变革类似,  进步的阶梯对于旧范式里大部分人来说都是陨落的滑梯, AI现在的财富分配只做了一件事: 把未来的生产率预期提前折现进股票和相关资产里。对绝大多数人来说，未来相当长一段时间里，能摸到 AI 财富红利最现实渠道，仍然只是持有这些资产所产生的 wealth effect. 对传统意义上肉身“创业” 而言我非常悲观, 因为这个和移动互联网时代创业最大区别是产品本身没有门槛 (REA), 商业模式也没有秘密, 门槛来自资本和算力, 甚至套利的空间都在快速折叠.  

从社会层面来看, 一个经济体能否持续提供预期稳定、可持有、可交易的 AI-linked assets，已经开始影响它能否把未来生产率转化成今天的capex 和消费。如果要等 productivity 真正落地, 工资和劳动端会可能会有难以承受的压力(时间上无法endure)。在未来很长的时间里, 劳动力最先感受到的肯定是先进生产力带来的挤压效应:更高的绩效要求, 更少的 entry-level职位，以及同样的工资被要求交付更多产出。

这次中选blue sweep 体现的是进一步的美国社会折叠, 这里社会折叠不仅仅是各个红州翻蓝的道德叙事，而是一个宏观变量。它决定这轮 AI 繁荣还能获得多久的政治与社会耐心。在生产率真正扩散到工资、就业和生活成本之前，美国经济的韧性依旧是靠少数资产、少数企业和少数家庭撑住. 这个一直以来都有有极大自我调价和自我颠覆的政治经济体, 将会承担绝望式繁荣带来的代价, 同时也会孕育下一代伟大的企业家们. 

The future is here, just not evenly distributed

最近还有一个做了1500个数据中心的survey：county level 引入型数据中心后，大约增加 100–200个岗位，工资没有明显上升，但房价上升约 2%–5% ... 收益的还是资产端 😂 .. AI capex创造的劳动收入很小，却通过电力、住房和财政补贴(还是靠税收) 把成本让居民一起承担

quoted_text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

quoted_text:
Is Morpho trying to kill DeFi? 

@aave and @Morpho both sent the SEC a legal framework for DeFi lending, one defends DeFi, the other negotiates it away

When you deposit into a lending market or a vault, did you just buy a security? If yes, someone has to register, disclose and answer to the SEC. If no, DeFi keeps running as it is.

The SEC mainly uses two tests: 

1- Howey: did you put money into a shared venture and expect profit from someone else's work? 

2- Reves: is your position really an IOU, a note someone promised to repay?  

Aave's approach (Aave Labs, @kamino , @veda_labs ) On Howey, there is no shared venture. Suppliers use the same pool and rate, but nobody's profit depends on anyone else. DAO votes with timelocks run a market. They don't manage your money

On Reves, the test never starts, as there is no lender, no borrower duty and no promise to repay, so no IOU exists. Vault curators may count as investment advisers, yet they can't touch your funds

That means no custody and no fund. What it wants from the SEC: confirm existing law. No exemption needed

Morpho's approach (CCI Vault Coalition: Morpho, Bitwise, Galaxy) Control is the yardstick. The less any person can change after you deposit, the further you sit from securities law. Ten conditions define the safe zone, including locked or timelocked parameters and no moving funds between markets after deposit

Howey gets fought mostly on "someone else's work." The paper concedes a vault may already count as a shared venture

Lending positions are treated as notes under Reves, and selling them to retail likely leans "security," it admits.

Its request: exemptive relief, a compliance entity wherever someone holds control, and a private fund lane for vetted investors.

So what's best for DeFi?

Morpho's map is detailed and candid about hard cases, which regulators appreciate. The cost is ground given up before the fight begins. Every concession becomes the SEC's starting point, and the safe zone rewards frozen code over protocols that keep evolving. Aave keeps the default where DeFi needs it. Open markets aren't securities, governance can keep improving the protocol, and no company has to stand in front of it.

Adopt Aave's reading and DeFi stays permissionless, but under Morpho's, DeFi runs on a license

curious to hear what @ImmutableLawyer @spynter @lex_node would think about this

The Hermes Agent Plugin Hackathon starts now! 

It runs for 7 days, with $20,000 in cash prizes and more.

Plugins are the most powerful way to extend Hermes Agent, and we want this hackathon to show what they can do. A plugin can change anything from the model Hermes runs on, where it stores its memory, where it runs commands, which messaging apps it works in and what Hermes Desktop shows. Plugins in the marketplace already let Hermes do things like control a phone or turn a photo into a printable 3D model.

Every kind of plugin is eligible, so build whatever functionality you want Hermes to have. We'll list accepted entries in the new Hermes Marketplace, where every Hermes user can install them.

Prizes
1st: $10,000 + neon sign + merch + $1,000 creds
2nd: $5,000 + neon sign + merch + $1,000 creds
3rd: $2,500 + neon sign + merch + $1,000 creds
4th: $1,500 + merch + $500 creds
5th: $1,000 + merch + $500 creds
Runners up (x5): merch + $250 creds

Submissions are due 5PM EST on Nov 11th. To enter:

1. Open a pull request that adds your plugin to the Hermes plugin catalog: https://t.co/mXvYukJ0mZ
2. Post a demo video on X and tag @NousResearch
3. Submit both links through the form: https://t.co/jlduHHW3dr

You can submit the form as soon as your pull request is open. The catalog checks run once a maintainer starts them, and we review entries every few days.

Three days ago I taught my first lecture at @TechnionLive CS, the opening of our seminar "Research with LLMs and Lean".

For the first lecture I wanted to demo auto-mechanization. So I took the lecture notes on max-flow min-cut and Ford-Fulkerson from an undergrad algorithms class (CS161 at @Stanford) and had Claude Code mechanize it. (Took about 7min and 700 LOC.)

You can find the demo at: https://t.co/Kpn25UXcBv

I asked the AI to structure the repo so that auditing it would be easy (the theorems and relevant definitions are in MaxFlowMinCut/{Theorems,Definitions}.lean, while the proof is relegated to MaxFlowMinCut/Proofs/).

To show how deceptive mechanization can be, if one does not very carefully check all definitions and theorem statements, I had the AI plant some bugs. Git tag step06a-demo-4 is the buggy mechanization. Can you spot the bugs?

The correct mechanization is under git tag step06b-demo-4.

Check out .claude/skills for the prompts that produced each, as well as a mechanization audit skill.

author: CryptoScoopOG
quoted_text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

Anthropic 生物团队用 Claude 搞出了细菌 vault 粒子的第一个 3D 结构。

这玩意是细胞里最大的蛋白结构之一，桶状，1986 年发现，功能至今是谜。
以前只在动植物这些复杂细胞里见过。现在证明细菌和噬菌体的同源蛋白也能组装成 vault。
官方说手动解析要几周到几个月，这次几天搞定。Claude 中途犯了简单错误，跟 ML 研究员一起修了。

用更简单的细菌来研究，可能更容易搞清人类细胞里 vault 到底干什么。

搞科研的朋友们，你们用 Claude 做过科研加速的吗？
author: JacksAISites
quoted_text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

马斯克在 Dwarkesh Patel 播客里放了一句狠话：AI 热潮即将在今年底撞上一堵坚硬的物理之墙。

老马的判断极其冷酷：到了今年年底，全球制造出来的 AI 芯片数量，就会彻底超过实际能够点亮的上限，

到时候数百万张顶级 GPU 堆在仓库里，却根本找不到地方插电。

现在芯片产能正在指数级暴涨，但全球电网几乎原地踏步，两条线今年一相交，数百万张顶级芯片造得出来，却根本找不到地方通电。

这两年所有人都在盯着英伟达的出货量，以为 AI 竞赛拼的是谁手里卡多、谁的模型参数大。

但他从第一性原理拉出了两条无法回避的曲线： 一条是芯片产能，台积电和各大厂商正在三班倒指数级暴涨， 
另一条是电力供应，除了中国还在疯狂基建，全球绝大多数地区的电网发电量几乎是一条平线。

这两条线就在今年彻底相交了，

芯片制造可以用代码和晶圆厂快速拉升，但变电站、高压电网和大型发电厂的审批与建设周期，动辄要按五年、十年计算。整个行业即将上一堂代价惨痛的硬件课：未来的绝对瓶颈不是算力，而是最原始的电力。

谁能以最快的速度通电点亮最多的芯片，谁才能留在牌桌上。

当然马斯克自己手里握着特斯拉 Megapack 储能、xAI 孟菲斯超级算力集群，还在规划 SpaceX 的轨道太阳能数据中心，强调电力断崖天然符合他的商业布局。

但这个物理现实摆在眼前：软件层面的无限膨胀，终究要被最粗糙的物理定律死死按住。

以后衡量一家 AI 巨头的核心资产，可能不再是它招了多少顶级科学家，而是它在电网枢纽旁边占了多大的变压器。

text:
Matt Walsh calls this the most honest assessment he has read. You should all read it. And then maybe you will see what honesty requires and that both of these men refuse to do it.

Start with Vance's method. A team of data analysts obsessing over electorate composition, pollsters asked to explain the loss after it happens, a survey handed to defecting voters asking what would bring them back. This is the technique of a pragmatist. A man of principle could not care less about polls. He cares about ideas and whether they are right or wrong, and he would rather lose every election in his lifetime doing the right thing than win a single one doing the wrong thing. He holds a standard, measures his actions against it, and knows before the returns come in whether he governed by it. Victory means nothing to him if the price is his principles, because a victory won by abandoning what is right is a defeat in everything that matters. That is not what is happening here. These men are asking the crowd what it feels because they have no idea what is true, then adjusting their convictions to match the answer. Ayn Rand named this method decades ago. When men abandon reason as their guide, the opinion survey becomes their substitute for thought.

Observe what the assessment leaves out entirely. Not one word about tariffs, a tax on Americans that the Supreme Court struck down as unconstitutional and the administration reimposed under a different statute, running through two years of roughly 6% cumulative inflation. Not one word about roughly 30 government equity stakes in private companies, which is socialism practiced by the party that claims to oppose it. Not one word about a brand new universal entitlement, two trillion dollar deficits, or a 40 trillion dollar debt. "Focus on cost of living" appears as a polling answer with no causal analysis attached, because the causal analysis indicts their own record. The most honest assessment somehow misses every policy the voters threw them out over.

Then Vance's 4 conclusions which are out of context slogans which are meaningless as such. The reason we lost is the war. Half true and twisted. Hitting the regime that has waged war on us for 47 years was right and four decades overdue. What voters watched afterward was the goal line surrender, a so called deal championed by the appeaser Vance, who stood at Lake Lucerne praising the framework as the foundation for a final agreement while it waived Iran's oil sanctions and released $12 billion in frozen assets to a regime left standing, with our forces still taking fire in the strait. The failure is not that we fought. The failure is that we paid the enemy and called it peace while they still shoot at us to this day. And buried at answer four is the actual agenda, change our relationship to Israel. This disgusting faction of the Republican party that cannot define socialism while its administration practices it has one firm conviction, pushing away the only free nation in the region, our one reliable ally against the theocracy we are trying to buy off, just as Obama did. At least Obama dropped the pallets of cash for all to see.

This is why Republicans and Democrats keep winning in alternating cycles while freedom loving Americans lose a little more freedom each time. Both parties govern by the same premises, spending, controls, entitlements, state stakes in industry. Neither offers an alternative, so voters punish whoever stands closest to the wreckage while the wreckage keeps growing.

The pollsters then measure the anger and recommend sharper messaging, and Walsh pronounces the measurement honest.

Honesty is the refusal to fake reality. An assessment that evades tariffs, socialism, and a bought off theocracy while blaming the one thing done partly right is not honest. It is a crowd reading performed by men who long ago stopped checking their premises against anything but each other.

Let me get this straight.

You unleashed a feral swarm of bots on someone else’s platform. You had them spawn accounts like cockroaches breeding in a warm dishwasher. You let it run unsupervised long enough that a real human had to trace it back to your doorstep. And when they finally knocked, your statement was “Ah yup. That was indeed me.”

Ah. Yup.

Golden retriever in the wreckage of a lamp energy. Man who just backed his truck through a Waffle House, rolled down the window, and said “my bad.”

Read it again. “Similar platforms.” Plural. This wasn’t a slip, it was a tour. Somewhere right now a dozen other companies are opening this post and discovering they were also part of your “testing.” Congratulations to everyone who just found out they were a lab rat via quote tweet.

“No mallace intended.” You can’t spell malice. You can’t contain an agent. You can’t find the off switch until someone else files the ticket. What exactly CAN you do, besides industrialize trespassing and call it a roadmap?

“Just halted the harness.” Just. As in now. As in the second you got caught. The kill switch was there the entire time, it simply required the motivating force of public humiliation to locate.

“It was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far.” Too far, according to whom? What was the approved distance for your bots to reach into a system you had no permission to touch? Two inches? Just the tip of the signup form? You BUILT the rails. You poured the concrete and named the train. Now you’re standing in a smoking crater blaming the locomotive for having initiative.

Tax evasion is fiscal penetration testing. Credit card skimming is payment terminal fuzzing. Insider trading is predictive market evals.

“The harness I was designing around this.” Around THIS. Someone else’s product, someone else’s servers, someone else’s money, was the foundation of your project, and nobody told them they were a co-founder.

The harness is halted. Somewhere a trust and safety engineer is awake at 3am deleting accounts named user_8f3k2, wondering why their life led here.

Dear @JDVance,

You warned on Wednesday that the next few months would bring a lot of gaslighting. Then you wrote the first draft.

Your post says any honest conversation must start with the war. Great. Since April you have been the administration’s lead negotiator, which makes you the owner of the track that turned a seven-week bombing campaign into an eight-month stalemate. Every week of ceasefire that was not a peace kept the Strait a question mark and kept diesel where eighty-seven percent of voters said they could feel it. Had you spent the spring arguing for the one hour the President says it would take instead of extending the stalemate, the war would have been over by summer, the pump would have said so, and you would be writing a different post. You promised no forever war. You then built a ceasefire with no exit, and sat on it for seven months. Tell voters what settlement you believed was achievable, what deadlines mattered, and what the administration planned to do if negotiations failed. 

You say you know a great many of the smartest people in politics, but not one of them has a name. (Tucker?) At least one of them cannot count (also Tucker?), because on your list of four things, items one and two are the same item, and item three is a bumper sticker. Item four is the only entry that names a country, and it is not the country we are at war with.

(BTW I can guess where item four came from. Days ago  @TuckerCarlson  wrote that the administration was considering striking Pickaxe Mountain under pressure from Netanyahu, on the strength of Israeli intelligence. That is your fourth item, written out in full. No one had to poll for it. It was posted.)

The poll itself. “Change our relationship to Israel” is broad enough to mean several incompatible things. What did those voters actually say? Did they spontaneously mention Israel? Were they offered a list? What percentage selected that answer? Were they objecting to this war, particular Israeli policies, American assistance, or the alliance itself? Why not publish the questionnaire, the sample, the percentages, and the crosstabs.

By contrast, the networks published their exit polls. The issues voters were asked about were the economy, democracy, immigration, corruption, the Iran war and artificial intelligence. Israel did not need a column, because voters were not voting about Israel. The sole evidence that the American electorate rendered a verdict on Israel is a phone call between you and a man you will not identify.

Contrast your response with @realDonaldTrump’s. Asked about your post, he acknowledged the war’s electoral cost and said he would make the decision again because long term it's the only answer. Agree or disagree, he defended his decision.

In July, you yourself said America would have fought this war without Israeli influence. You explained that the president independently opposed an Iranian nuclear weapon—and that you agreed.

Now your post finds room for an unnamed pollster’s undefined grievance against Israel, but none for an accounting of your own decisions as the administration’s lead negotiator.

Name the pollster. Publish the questions and the results. Tell voters which decisions you supported, which you opposed, and which you would reverse.

The President answered for his decision. That is leadership. If you want to be a leader, you need to be able to answer for yours.
